docs.text: GeoDatalytics is a web-based platform designed to enable AI-driven analytics and simulation in urban environments. It empowers analysts, planners, and data scientists with the tools they need to ingest, explore, simulate, transform, and visualize complex urban data—all in one integrated environment. GeoDatalytics can support diverse use cases related to urban environments, enabling comprehensive data visualization and simulation capabilities that enhance the resilience of infrastructure and foster sustainable urban solutions. Key Capabilities Scenario-based analytics : explore flood impact analysis, transportation disruption, infrastructure risk assessment, etc. AI & simulation workflows : run pretrained models on geospatial and network data to generate actionable insights Interactive visualization : explore multiscale results through interactive maps, custom layer styling, and side-by-side comparison Multi-source data integration : ingest vector, raster, and tabular data representing roads, utilities, floods, amenities, elevation, satellite imagery, sensor data, etc. Collaborative project management : configure your projects to include relevant datasets, set permissions for your collaborators, and save informative views for others to see your results

The Analytics panel allows you to run any kind of complex task that takes data as input and/or generates new data as an output. These tasks can include but are not limited to: AI inference, simulation, network analysis, and dataset generation. The Analytics panel is intended to be an abstract interface to support many different kinds of tasks. The tasks you will need depend on your use case, so you may need to implement new tasks. If you would like to write the code yourself, you can refer to the Custom Analytics documentation and add the task to a self-hosted instance of GeoDatalytics. Or you can Contact Kitware so we can help support your use case. We can implement your custom task and add it to the public GeoDatalytics instance at geodatalytics.kitware.com or help you deploy a private instance with your custom task enabled. GeoDatalytics already has six different tasks available to explore a few example use cases. These six tasks each demonstrate different capabilities, providing a small sample of the potential afforded by the analytics features. This documentation will describe the basic controls of the Analytics panel through one of the six tasks, and then the remaining five tasks will be explored through an example use case. Basic Controls In the Analytics panel’s initial state, a list of available task types is displayed. A search bar allows you to filter the task types by name. An information icon is shown to the right of each task type name; hovering over the icon will display a tooltip with the description of the task type. Clicking on a task type from the list will open the main panel view for that task type. This tutorial will explore the “Imagery: Ask Qwen” task, which allows you to ask Qwen 3.5, a large language model, a question about an aerial imagery raster layer. The main task view has a title row which includes the name of the task type and an “X” button to close the task and return to the task list. If the task type has any additional information you need to know, an expandable “Details” section will also be visible. For this task, the details section explains about the model being used. Below the title row is a tabbed interface with a “Run New” and a “View Existing” tab. The “Run New” tab displays a form where you can specify inputs. Submitting the form will spawn a task. The “View Existing” tab displays a list of previous runs. Each run in the list can be expanded to show its inputs, status, and outputs. Note If you do not have write access on the current project, you will not have access to run new tasks, so you will not see the tabs. You will only see the content of the “View Existing” tab. Run New Tab The “Run New” tab displays a form to specify various inputs required for running that particular task. The controls visible will depend on which task type you are going to run. There are three basic types of controls. Selection control with a search function to filter the list of available options Numeric slider with a set minimum, maximum, and step Free text input There is also a specialized type of selection control if the input requires a region. This specialized control will show regions on the map as you hover over options in the list and will keep a region visible on the map once it has been selected. The region input control has two additional buttons on the right. The filter icon can be clicked to toggle option filtering on and off. When option filtering is enabled, the options shown in the dropdown will be limited to regions that intersect the map’s current viewport. The plus-polygon icon to the right of the input, when clicked, will initiate draw mode. When draw mode is enabled an “X” icon will be shown in the same place to cancel the draw. When draw mode is enabled, you can click anywhere on the map to place points for a closed polygon. Close the polygon by clicking on your initial point or pressing the “Enter” key. You may also press the “Esc” key to start your drawing over if you make a mistake. Once the polygon is closed, a text input will appear below the region selection control. You must supply a name for the new region in the text box before you can use it as an input for your task run. After you enter a unique and informative name, press “Enter” or click the blue arrow button to the right of the text input, and your region will be saved. Your newly created region will also be automatically selected in the region selection control. Once you have specified a value for all required inputs, you may click the “Run Analysis” button to spawn the task. Once the task is spawned, the panel will automatically switch to the “View Existing” tab so you can monitor the progress of your task run. View Existing Tab The “View Existing” tab displays a list of all previous runs of the current task type. Each run has a timestamp and a title determined by the inputs. Each run can be expanded to show its inputs, status, and outputs. For example, this completed run of the “Imagery: Ask Qwen” shows a table with the four inputs provided for the run. Inputs that can be shown on the map have “Show” buttons next to them. Once clicked, that data will be shown on the map and the button will be replaced with a “Hide” button. Below the inputs table, the status of the task shows it took about 4.5 minutes to complete. Lastly, below the status, the task outputs are shown. For the “Imagery: Ask Qwen” task, the only output is a markdown text response. We’ll see other output types in the following section as we explore other task types in an example use case. When a task is still running, no outputs will be shown yet. A loading bar will appear and the status will state the current step of the task. The status will update automatically as the task progresses. For shorter tasks, you may just want to watch the status while you wait for the task to complete. But for longer running tasks, you may wish to work on other things while your task is running. Below the status, there is a “Notify Me Once Completed” button. Once you click this button, you will be subscribed to the task and an email will be sent to you once the task is completed. Once the task is completed, the task display will automatically update to show the outputs. Task Chain Example Use Case To explore the remaining five remaining analytics tasks, this section will follow an example use case examining the impact of a simulated flood on a transportation network. The tasks in this use case are chained together, where the output of one task is used as the input to the next task. Task 1: Create Road Network We begin with the “Create Road Network” task, which takes only one input. We only need to specify the name of the target location. This task will leverage osmnx to generate a dataset of the roads in the target location. The road system will be represented with a network of nodes and edges. Once the task completes, the roads dataset is listed in the task’s outputs. Clicking the “Show” button will add the layer to the map. After adjusting the layer’s style a bit, the resulting road network looks like this. Zoomed out, the full result network looks like this: Task 2: AI Flood Simulation For the second task, we’ll simulate an extreme flood event in the future. We developed the “AI Flood Simulation” task in collaboration with the Sustainability and Data Sciences Laboratory at Northeastern University . The simulation module is open source and available on GitHub . This task requires several inputs: An initial condition set. Initial conditions "001", "002", and "003" start real-world emissions from year 1850 with the climate state from the 1001st, 1021st, and 1041st year of a pre-industrial control simulation. Since Earth's climate undergoes multi-year and multi-decadal cycles, the different initializations reveal the range of possible climates in real-world years 2031 and beyond. A target time period. Available options are “2031-2050” and “2041-2060”. A hydrograph chart. This simple bell curve represents the proportional discharge over time of a river during an extreme flood event. There are two available hydrograph charts, which can be viewed in the Charts Panel . The first represents the Charles River measured from Waltham, and the second represents a longer stretch of the Charles River, including more upriver tributaries. Potential evapotranspiration percentile. Percentile value between 0 and 100 representing the maximum amount of water that can evaporate in accordance with certain atmospheric conditions. Soil moisture percentile. Percentile value between 0 and 100 representing soil moisture in the unsaturated soil levels above the water table. Ground water percentile. Percentile value between 0 and 100 representing the amount of water in the saturated rock and soil layers below the water table. Annual probability. Probability of the flood expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1. The probability expresses the severity of the flood. An annual probability of 0.01 represents a 1-in-100 year flood, and an annual probability of 0.25 represents a 1-in-4 year flood. After selecting a set of inputs and spawning the task, the AI flood simulation module built by Northeastern University will run. This run was completed in 29 seconds. The resulting flood dataset is shown in the outputs table, along with the computed values for the total precipitation in millimeters and the discharge rate in cubic feet per second. Clicking the “Show” button next to the flood dataset will add the flood to the map. The flood layer is a multiframe layer, so the frame slider allows us to scrub through the frames of the flood. Each frame is an hour over a 24-hour period. This screenshot shows the seventh hour of the flood, which is the peak, in accordance with the hydrograph we selected. Task 3: Flood Network Failure The next task will use the outputs of the previous two tasks as inputs. The flood network failure task examines how a selected network will be affected by a simulated flood. We’ll select the road network we generated and the flood we just simulated. This task takes a few additional inputs to calibrate when a node goes out of service due to flooding. The depth tolerance expresses how much water (in meters) a node can tolerate. The station radius expresses how much area is covered by a node; the area around the node point with this radius (in meters) is considered part of the node. A node will be considered out of service if flood levels exceed the depth tolerance in any area covered by the node. One thing to note about this task is the time complexity of this calculation. This task won’t take long for a sparse network like the MBTA Rapid Transit system, but for a dense network like the road system, this task can take some time. When this task run completes, the output section includes an item labeled “animation” with a “Show” button. Clicking the “Show” button will open the Networks Panel and load the animation steps. Once the animation is loaded, the Networks Panel will display a slider to scrub through the animation, as well as play/pause/rewind buttons to step through the animation at a regular interval. See the Networks Panel documentation to learn more about the controls for network animations. As the animation proceeds, both the flood layer and the network layer will update. For each hour in the 24-hour flood period, the animation will show the corresponding frame of the flood layer and update the network style according to the node states during that hour. The following video shows the full flood animation resulting from this task run: Task 4: Network Recovery The next task in the chain is the network recovery task, which accepts the output of the previous task as input. This task will evaluate all the nodes that went out of service during the failure simulation and evaluate the best order to prioritize node recoveries according to a given metric. The available metric options pertain to different network topology principles. For this run, we select the task result we just ran and the “degree” metric, which evaluates each node by the number of edges connected to it. The first output is a “gcc chart”, and clicking the “Show” button next to that output will open the Charts Panel and display a chart. This chart depicts how the number of deactivated nodes and the size of the network’s greatest connected component (GCC) change over time as the flood and recovery events proceed. In the chart below, timesteps 0-23 represent the flood event; the number of deactivated nodes increases (red line) and the size of the greatest connected component decreases (blue line), and then they stay static as the flood recedes. Then the recovery phase begins, and with one node recovered each timestep, in the order determined by the selected metric, the number of deactivated nodes decreases and the size of the greatest connected component increases. The second output of this task is an animation similar to the one shown as the output of the previous task. This animation will show nodes coming back online one at a time, ordered by the selected metric. The third output of this task is a resiliency score between 0 and 1. The resiliency score represents the area under the GCC curve with outages over the area under the curve without outages. This metric is related to the overall resilience of the network against outages. A more highly connected network will maintain a large GCC even with many outages, and will therefore have a higher resiliency score. The resiliency score value we received for this run with the roads network was 0.83. We can compare that to a previous run on the MBTA Rapid Transit network, which has much less redundancy; that run received a resilience score of 0.37. Task 5: Flood Uncertainty Quantification The final task we’ll explore in this use case offers a way to validate the flood simulation step. This task was developed by our collaborators at Northeastern University. You can select three previous runs of the flood simulation task, and this task will calculate a handful of error statistics from their outputs for maximum precipitation and discharge rate. Since this task is just a relatively simple computation, it completes in less than a second. It has several numeric outputs that can be used to quantify uncertainty among the three floods. Conclusion The six task types explored in this documentation demonstrate the range and potential of the analytics features. Some tasks are more complex simulations, some leverage AI models, and some are straightforward computation. The analytics features are adaptable to various task types, and adding new tasks can be achieved with the addition of a python class. If you are interested in implementing your own task, refer to the Advanced Documentation for Custom Analytics . Otherwise, Contact Kitware and tell us about your use case so we can write new task types to support you.

docs.text: Introduction Interactive Documentation GeoDatalytics Models Python Example Introduction While the web user interface provides controls to accomplish basic tasks for common use cases, there are some actions that cannot be performed in the user interface. Similarly, some advanced use cases might call for automation of certain actions. For these circumstances, the application programming interface (API) can be leveraged to fetch, create, update, and delete objects in the database, as well as spawn analytics tasks and await their results. This guide is intended for Python developers with a basic understanding of requests. Note Please use caution when interacting with any API endpoints that perform database write operations. If you have any questions about the GeoDatalytics API, Contact Kitware so we can help support your use case. Interactive Documentation GeoDatalytics adheres to the OpenAPI specification and uses Swagger for its API documentation. The full API documentation can be accessed at the GeoDatalytics API Docs , which shows a list of all endpoints. Expanding an endpoint will show the schema for any expected inputs and outputs. The “Try It Out” button will enable form controls to create and send a request to that endpoint. Response bodies are displayed as formatted JSON and can be copied to the clipboard or downloaded. This interactive documentation will use your authentication if you have signed in to GeoDatalytics in another tab. Otherwise, your API access will be anonymous and limited to only public projects. GeoDatalytics Models The API endpoints are organized into groups by the model they pertain to. Before proceeding with API interactions, you should know how the GeoDatalytics models are organized. Each model has a unique purpose, attribute set, and relationships to other models. Projects are the top level of organization. A project has a set of allowed users with different permission levels. A project can have zero or more datasets, charts, task results, bookmarks, and colormaps. Datasets and charts can have a relationship to a file item, which contains the original file content before conversion to a standard format. Some datasets can have a relationship to a network, which has relationships to network nodes and network edges. A dataset must have one or more layers to show on the map, and a layer style can be created for a particular layer to control how that layer is visualized. Each layer must have one or more layer frames. Each layer frame must have a related raster data or vector data, which contains the converted, standardized data that is optimized for visualization. For vector data, this includes one or more individual vector feature objects. Some vector data may also have related region objects, which represent polygon features with specialized behavior. The only model shown in the diagram above not related to any other models is the basemap. Basemaps are global objects containing a configuration for map tiles to show general geography. They are not constrained by the project. Only some of these models have dedicated API endpoints; other models are more hidden implementations. There are even more hidden models not present in this diagram. Some models that do have API endpoints are read-only. For example, the vector and raster data models have read only endpoints for visualization, but they can only be created during a dataset conversion task, so they do not have a creation endpoint. Most basic API use cases will only involve one or two models. If your use case is advanced and requires managing multiple model relationships, Contact Kitware so we can help support your use case. Python Example Interacting with the API via python scripts can be especially useful for automating tasks. For example, if you have a source of continuously updating sensor data, you could write a script to update a particular chart with the latest data and schedule your script to run once a day. The following python example demonstrates such a use case. Your use case will likely require the use of other endpoints, but you will likely want all your requests to be authenticated, so at minimum you will need to use the token endpoint in a similar manner. docs.text: While the web user interface provides controls to accomplish basic tasks for common use cases, there are some actions that cannot be performed in the user interface. Similarly, some advanced use cases might call for automation of certain actions. For these circumstances, the application programming interface (API) can be leveraged to fetch, create, update, and delete objects in the database, as well as spawn analytics tasks and await their results. This guide is intended for Python developers with a basic understanding of requests. Note Please use caution when interacting with any API endpoints that perform database write operations. If you have any questions about the GeoDatalytics API, Contact Kitware so we can help support your use case.
docs.title: Introduction

docs.text: GeoDatalytics adheres to the OpenAPI specification and uses Swagger for its API documentation. The full API documentation can be accessed at the GeoDatalytics API Docs , which shows a list of all endpoints. Expanding an endpoint will show the schema for any expected inputs and outputs. The “Try It Out” button will enable form controls to create and send a request to that endpoint. Response bodies are displayed as formatted JSON and can be copied to the clipboard or downloaded. This interactive documentation will use your authentication if you have signed in to GeoDatalytics in another tab. Otherwise, your API access will be anonymous and limited to only public projects.
docs.title: Interactive Documentation

docs.text: The API endpoints are organized into groups by the model they pertain to. Before proceeding with API interactions, you should know how the GeoDatalytics models are organized. Each model has a unique purpose, attribute set, and relationships to other models. Projects are the top level of organization. A project has a set of allowed users with different permission levels. A project can have zero or more datasets, charts, task results, bookmarks, and colormaps. Datasets and charts can have a relationship to a file item, which contains the original file content before conversion to a standard format. Some datasets can have a relationship to a network, which has relationships to network nodes and network edges. A dataset must have one or more layers to show on the map, and a layer style can be created for a particular layer to control how that layer is visualized. Each layer must have one or more layer frames. Each layer frame must have a related raster data or vector data, which contains the converted, standardized data that is optimized for visualization. For vector data, this includes one or more individual vector feature objects. Some vector data may also have related region objects, which represent polygon features with specialized behavior. The only model shown in the diagram above not related to any other models is the basemap. Basemaps are global objects containing a configuration for map tiles to show general geography. They are not constrained by the project. Only some of these models have dedicated API endpoints; other models are more hidden implementations. There are even more hidden models not present in this diagram. Some models that do have API endpoints are read-only. For example, the vector and raster data models have read only endpoints for visualization, but they can only be created during a dataset conversion task, so they do not have a creation endpoint. Most basic API use cases will only involve one or two models. If your use case is advanced and requires managing multiple model relationships, Contact Kitware so we can help support your use case.

docs.text: Introduction Creating New Charts via API Introduction While GeoDatalytics is primarily focused on visualizing geospatial data on a map, the Charts panel also allows you to visualize tabular data with line charts. Chart data can be created during an Analytics task or uploaded via the API. Currently, chart creation via the user interface is not yet supported. The Charts panel is a read-only view of charts in the current project. In its default state, the Charts panel shows a list of all Chart objects included in the current project. Each item shows the chart name, followed by two icons. The information icon shows the chart’s description when the mouse hovers over it. The vertical three dots icon, when clicked, will open the details dialog for that chart. The details dialog for any given chart will show the name, id, description, metadata, and related objects like files. If there are any related files, you can download them from this dialog. Clicking on any chart in the Charts panel will display an interactive visualization of the chart data. You can hover over any data point to see its value. In the top right corner of the chart display, there are two icons. The download icon will initiate a download of the chart data, formatted as JSON. The X button will close the chart visualization and return to the list of charts. Note that if the chart was converted from a CSV, the download button in the top right will not download the original CSV file; it will download a version of the data formatted for visualization. The original CSV can only be downloaded from the details dialog. Note that some charts are more dense than others, and may require that you resize the Charts panel to see the data properly, since the Charts panel is relatively small by default. To learn more about resizing panels, see the Panel Controls documentation. For chart data that is particularly dense, with more than 500 labels along the x-axis, only the first 500 labels will be shown by default and a range slider will appear below the chart to control the current x-axis window. Creating New Charts via API While creating a chart is not yet supported in the user interface, you can create new charts via the API. The API offers two modes of chart creation: direct data entry and file conversion. Direct data entry is recommended, as it is the simpler approach. File conversion is a more advanced approach with more steps. The following code example demonstrates chart creation with direct data entry: import json import requests from datetime import datetime with requests.Session() as session: token = session.post(f'{base_url}/api/v1/token/', dict( username=username, password=password, )).json().get('token') session.headers.update({ 'Authorization': f'Token {token}', 'Accept': 'application/json', }) my_new_chart = dict( name='Example Chart', description='Line chart with two datasets uploaded via API', project=project_id, metadata=json.dumps(dict( uploaded=datetime.now().strftime('YYYY-mm-dd HH:MM:SS'), nested=dict( example=True, ), )), chart_data=json.dumps(dict( # Pass x-axis labels labels=['Sunday', 'Monday', 'Tuesday', 'Wednesday', 'Thursday', 'Friday', 'Saturday'], # Pass one or more datasets containing y-values datasets=[ # One blue line for "Focus Time" dict( data=[0.5, 3, 4, 5, 3, 1, 0], label='Focus Time', borderColor='#0000ff', backgroundColor='#0000ff', ), # One red line for "Relaxation" dict( data=[7.5, 4, 3, 2, 4, 6, 8], label='Relaxation', borderColor='#ff0000', backgroundColor='#ff0000', ) ], )), chart_options=json.dumps(dict( x_title='Weekday', y_title='Number of Hours', chart_title='Weekly Time Management', )) ) r = session.post(f'{base_url}/api/v1/charts/', my_new_chart) print(r.json()) The screenshot below shows the resulting chart object in the Charts panel. The next example shows chart creation with file conversion. The file conversion approach is more advanced, so the direct data entry approach is recommended for most use cases. However, this approach does have the advantage of creating a related file object, which can be downloaded from the details dialog. Use this approach if you would like to allow users to download the original CSV contents of the chart. This example references a file called example_chart.csv , which contains the following comma-separated values: weekday,focus_time,relaxation Sunday,0.5,7.5 Monday,3,4 Tuesday,4,3 Wednesday,5,2 Thursday,3,4 Friday,1,6 Saturday,0,8 For this example, you will need to install the django-s3-file-field-client to complete the file upload process. pip install django-s3-file-field-client The code below will result in the creation of a new chart, identical to the one above. This process involves more steps than the previous example. First, the chart object is created without any chart_data specified. Second, the contents of the CSV file are uploaded via a specialized client from django-s3-file-field-client , and a file key is obtained from that upload. Third, a file object related to the chart is created with the file key. Fourth, a conversion task is spawned; that task will run asynchronously on the server, so a TaskResult object is returned in that response. You can track the progress of the conversion task by getting the status of that TaskResult object. The conversion task will parse the contents of the uploaded CSV to fill in the chart_data on the chart object. Once the conversion task is complete, you can view the chart in the Charts panel just as you would for the previous example. import json import requests import mimetypes from datetime import datetime from pathlib import Path from s3_file_field_client import S3FileFieldClient with requests.Session() as session: token = session.post(f'{base_url}/api/v1/token/', dict( username=username, password=password, )).json().get('token') session.headers.update({ 'Authorization': f'Token {token}', 'Accept': 'application/json', }) my_new_chart = dict( name='Example Chart', description='Line chart with two datasets uploaded via API', project=project_id, metadata=json.dumps(dict( uploaded=datetime.now().strftime('YYYY-mm-dd HH:MM:SS'), nested=dict( example=True, ), )), chart_options=json.dumps(dict( x_title='Weekday', y_title='Number of Hours', chart_title='Weekly Time Management', )), ) r = session.post(f'{base_url}/api/v1/charts/', my_new_chart) chart_id = r.json().get('id') # Upload file contents to server file_path = Path('example_chart.csv') s3ff_client = S3FileFieldClient( f'{base_url}/api/v1/s3-upload/', session, ) with file_path.open('rb') as f: file_field_value = s3ff_client.upload_file( file_stream=f, file_name=file_path.name, file_content_type=mimetypes.guess_type(file_path)[0], field_id='core.FileItem.file', # this value is the same for all file uploads ) # Create File object my_new_file = dict( name=file_path.name, # can match local file name but doesn't need to chart=chart_id, file=file_field_value, # pass the value we got from the file content upload file_type='csv', file_size=file_path.stat().st_size, metadata=json.dumps(dict( uploaded=datetime.now().strftime('YYYY-mm-dd HH:MM:SS'), )), ) r = session.post(f'{base_url}/api/v1/files/', my_new_file) # Spawn conversion task on the chart r = session.post(f'{base_url}/api/v1/charts/{chart_id}/convert/', dict( conversion_options=json.dumps(dict( labels='weekday', datasets=['focus_time', 'relaxation'], palette=dict( focus_time='blue', relaxation='red', ), )) )) # response contains a task result object to track the progress of the conversion print(r.json())

docs.text: Introduction Bookmarks Menu Basemap Menu Creating a new basemap Panel Visibility Screenshot Menu Map Autofit Theme Toggle Help Menu Introduction GeoDatalytics leverages MapLibre to provide an interactive map display in the main interface. By default, MapLibre provides mouse and keyboard controls to zoom and pan the map. Mouse controls Scroll up/down to zoom in/out Click and drag to pan Keyboard Controls +/- to zoom in/out Arrow keys to pan If you add a vector data layer to the map, you can click on any vector feature to display a map tooltip with a list of the feature’s properties. This map tooltip may also show some additional controls for specialized features like network nodes. In addition to the basic MapLibre controls, GeoDatalytics provides advanced controls in the toolbar in the top right corner of the map area. This controls bar includes a set of icon buttons that offer advanced features. From left to right, these buttons offer the bookmarks menu, basemap menu, panel visibility menu, screenshot menu, map autofit button, theme toggle button, and help menu. The following sections will explain each of these buttons. Bookmarks Menu The first icon in the controls bar will only appear if a project is selected. Hovering over this icon will display the bookmarks menu, which allows you to view the bookmarks that exist on the current project. If you have write permission on the project, this menu also allows you to save your current view state as a bookmark. Bookmarks allow you to create shortcuts to informative visualizations that you can share with others who have read permission on your project. These bookmarks can be shared and loaded via URL, so you can quickly reload common visualizations. The state saved for a bookmark includes the application theme, basemap, map position, selected layers, current layer styles, sidebar states, and panel configuration. If your current project does not yet have any bookmarks, the menu will state that “No saved bookmarks exist for this project.” The “Save current view as bookmark” button at the top of the menu, when clicked, will open a dialog form to create a new bookmark for this project. Note If you are not logged in or otherwise lack write permission on the current project, you will not have access to create a new bookmark, so that button will be absent from the bookmarks menu. The bookmark creation dialog is a simple form with only one field. You only need to specify a unique name for the bookmark. Below that, a generated thumbnail for the bookmark will be shown. The thumbnail is simply a screenshot of the application taken right before the dialog opens. Once you supply a name and click the “Create” button to submit the form, you will be redirected to the bookmark’s URL and the view state will be reloaded. This may include a slight repositioning of the map to the nearest zoom level. Anyone who visits this bookmark’s URL will see the same thing as long as they have read permission on the project. Opening the bookmarks menu again will show that the newly created bookmark now appears in the list. The list item includes the thumbnail, bookmark name, a trash icon, and a share icon. When you load a bookmark, the bookmark icon in the controls bar will be filled in to show a bookmark is active. Clicking on the trash icon will open a dialog asking you to confirm whether you want to delete the bookmark. Clicking on the share icon will copy the bookmark’s URL to your clipboard. Basemap Menu The basemap is the set of tiles displayed to show the underlying geography before any dataset layers are added. The basemap menu, which is displayed when you hover over the second icon in the controls bar, allows you to set the current basemap. GeoDatalytics has several basemap options built-in, but you can also create your own. Note If you are not logged in, you will not have access to create a new basemap, so that option will not be present in the basemap list. Clicking on any available option in the basemap list will switch the basemap and load the new tiles. The “None” basemap option does not have any tiles, so it does not show a preview. Selecting this option is equivalent to turning off the basemap. The map will appear blank except for any data layers. The previews shown next to each basemap option will be created with the same bounds as the main map, so zooming into an area of interest on the main map will cause the previews to show the same area of interest. The previews are also mini interactive maps, so you can use the mouse map controls to pan and zoom if your mouse is over a preview map. Keyboard controls are disabled for the previews. Creating a new basemap At the top of the basemap menu, there is an option to “+ Create Custom Basemap”. Clicking on this option will open the basemap creation dialog. The basemap creation dialog displays a form asking you to name and configure the new basemap. The basemap configuration section has two tabs; you can either set a Tile URL or a MapLibre Style JSON. By default, the Tile URL tab is active; this method is more simple and common. This tab shows an example Tile URL value, an expandable section with advanced instructions, and an input to supply your URL. When the advanced instructions section is expanded, some additional information is displayed about using a public API key in your tile URL. Below the tile URL input, a map preview is shown so that you can confirm whether your URL works. If no preview appears, your tile URL may be incorrect or the target tile server may be down. In the screenshot below, the provided example URL has been pasted into the input, and the preview shows an interactive map. This map can pan and zoom with mouse controls (or with keyboard controls if you first focus the preview by clicking on it or tabbing to it). Switching to the “MapLibre Style JSON” tab will display some explanatory text, a JSON editor, and a similar map preview area. This tab explains that you must “Supply a JSON that adheres to the Maplibre Style Spec . Style spec can be supplied directly as JSON or as a URL string that references a publicly accessible JSON file”. The linked MapLibre documentation explains what their style specification entails. This tab also provides an example value, so the screenshot below shows that the example value has been pasted into the JSON editor input, and the preview shows an interactive map. This example value is a URL pointing to a publicly accessible JSON file with a full MapLibre style specification. You may also specify the basemap style directly with JSON. In the screenshot below, the JSON editor input has a simple style specification; this is the same specification used for the “Basic Dark” builtin basemap. As you type in the JSON editor, your style specification will be validated prior to creating the interactive preview. An informative error message will be displayed if you fail to meet the style specification requirements. The screenshot below shows the same style specification with the “layers” property removed. Instead of an interactive preview, the following message is displayed: “Error: missing required property ‘layers’”. Once your preview works properly and has the desired style, you may click the “Create” button at the bottom of the dialog. Your custom basemap will appear in the list in the basemap menu. Note All users will be able to see and use your custom basemap once it has been created. Panel Visibility The third icon in the controls menu offers a simple list of checkbox controls. Each item in the list corresponds to a UI panel and the checkbox controls the visibility of that panel. If you close a panel with the ‘X’ button in the top right corner of the panel, you can open it again from this menu. Screenshot Menu The fourth icon in the controls bar is a camera; hovering over this icon will display the screenshot menu. This simple menu only has a few controls: A checkbox labelled “Map Only”. This checkbox is unchecked by default. When this checkbox is checked, the resulting screenshot will exclude the sidebars, control bar, and any floating panels. Only map elements (including the map tooltip) will be shown. A “Copy image to clipboard” button which, when clicked, will take a screenshot and copy the resulting image to your clipboard. A “Save image” button which, when clicked, will take a screenshot and use your browser’s default behavior to save the image to disk. On some browsers, this may go straight to your Downloads folder. On other browsers, a filesystem dialog may appear to prompt you for the location to which the screenshot should be saved. By default, the image will be named “geodatalytics_screenshot.png”. For both copied and saved screenshots, a camera flash animation will appear to indicate that the screenshot has been captured. Map Autofit The fifth icon in the controls bar is a button to automatically fit the bounds of the map to the set of currently visible layers. In this case, a “visible” layer is any layer that is added to the Selected Layers panel and does not have its visibility toggled off. A layer can be visible even if it is not in your current viewport. Keep in mind that if you have multiple visible layers, clicking this button will fly the map to a position that shows the union of the bounds of all of those layers. If your visible layers are geographically far apart, this button will likely be less useful. If you only have one visible layer, this button will autofit the map bounds to just that layer. This can be especially useful if you don’t know where the layer should appear on the map and want to find the location quickly. If you have not yet added any layers to the map, this button does nothing. Theme Toggle The sixth icon in the controls bar is a button to toggle the application theme between light and dark modes. Help Menu The seventh and final icon in the controls bar shows a simple help menu when hovered. This help menu has a button to show a small tutorial of the interface, and it summarizes the map’s mouse and keyboard controls explained in the introduction above.

The state saved for a bookmark includes the application theme, basemap, map position, selected layers, current layer styles, sidebar states, and panel configuration. If your current project does not yet have any bookmarks, the menu will state that “No saved bookmarks exist for this project.” The “Save current view as bookmark” button at the top of the menu, when clicked, will open a dialog form to create a new bookmark for this project. Note If you are not logged in or otherwise lack write permission on the current project, you will not have access to create a new bookmark, so that button will be absent from the bookmarks menu. The bookmark creation dialog is a simple form with only one field. You only need to specify a unique name for the bookmark. Below that, a generated thumbnail for the bookmark will be shown. The thumbnail is simply a screenshot of the application taken right before the dialog opens. Once you supply a name and click the “Create” button to submit the form, you will be redirected to the bookmark’s URL and the view state will be reloaded. When you load a bookmark, the bookmark icon in the controls bar will be filled in to show a bookmark is active. Clicking on the trash icon will open a dialog asking you to confirm whether you want to delete the bookmark. Clicking on the share icon will copy the bookmark’s URL to your clipboard.

docs.text: The basemap is the set of tiles displayed to show the underlying geography before any dataset layers are added. The basemap menu, which is displayed when you hover over the second icon in the controls bar, allows you to set the current basemap. GeoDatalytics has several basemap options built-in, but you can also create your own. Note If you are not logged in, you will not have access to create a new basemap, so that option will not be present in the basemap list. Clicking on any available option in the basemap list will switch the basemap and load the new tiles. The “None” basemap option does not have any tiles, so it does not show a preview. Selecting this option is equivalent to turning off the basemap. The map will appear blank except for any data layers. The previews shown next to each basemap option will be created with the same bounds as the main map, so zooming into an area of interest on the main map will cause the previews to show the same area of interest. The previews are also mini interactive maps, so you can use the mouse map controls to pan and zoom if your mouse is over a preview map. Keyboard controls are disabled for the previews.

docs.text: At the top of the basemap menu, there is an option to “+ Create Custom Basemap”. Clicking on this option will open the basemap creation dialog. The basemap creation dialog displays a form asking you to name and configure the new basemap. The basemap configuration section has two tabs; you can either set a Tile URL or a MapLibre Style JSON. By default, the Tile URL tab is active; this method is more simple and common. This tab shows an example Tile URL value, an expandable section with advanced instructions, and an input to supply your URL. When the advanced instructions section is expanded, some additional information is displayed about using a public API key in your tile URL. Below the tile URL input, a map preview is shown so that you can confirm whether your URL works. If no preview appears, your tile URL may be incorrect or the target tile server may be down. In the screenshot below, the provided example URL has been pasted into the input, and the preview shows an interactive map. This map can pan and zoom with mouse controls (or with keyboard controls if you first focus the preview by clicking on it or tabbing to it). Switching to the “MapLibre Style JSON” tab will display some explanatory text, a JSON editor, and a similar map preview area. This tab explains that you must “Supply a JSON that adheres to the Maplibre Style Spec . Style spec can be supplied directly as JSON or as a URL string that references a publicly accessible JSON file”. The linked MapLibre documentation explains what their style specification entails. This tab also provides an example value, so the screenshot below shows that the example value has been pasted into the JSON editor input, and the preview shows an interactive map. This example value is a URL pointing to a publicly accessible JSON file with a full MapLibre style specification. You may also specify the basemap style directly with JSON. In the screenshot below, the JSON editor input has a simple style specification; this is the same specification used for the “Basic Dark” builtin basemap. As you type in the JSON editor, your style specification will be validated prior to creating the interactive preview. An informative error message will be displayed if you fail to meet the style specification requirements. The screenshot below shows the same style specification with the “layers” property removed. Instead of an interactive preview, the following message is displayed: “Error: missing required property ‘layers’”. Once your preview works properly and has the desired style, you may click the “Create” button at the bottom of the dialog. Your custom basemap will appear in the list in the basemap menu. Note All users will be able to see and use your custom basemap once it has been created.
docs.title: Creating a new basemap

docs.text: The third icon in the controls menu offers a simple list of checkbox controls. Each item in the list corresponds to a UI panel and the checkbox controls the visibility of that panel. If you close a panel with the ‘X’ button in the top right corner of the panel, you can open it again from this menu.
docs.title: Panel Visibility

docs.text: The fourth icon in the controls bar is a camera; hovering over this icon will display the screenshot menu. This simple menu only has a few controls: A checkbox labelled “Map Only”. This checkbox is unchecked by default. When this checkbox is checked, the resulting screenshot will exclude the sidebars, control bar, and any floating panels. Only map elements (including the map tooltip) will be shown. A “Copy image to clipboard” button which, when clicked, will take a screenshot and copy the resulting image to your clipboard. A “Save image” button which, when clicked, will take a screenshot and use your browser’s default behavior to save the image to disk. On some browsers, this may go straight to your Downloads folder. On other browsers, a filesystem dialog may appear to prompt you for the location to which the screenshot should be saved. By default, the image will be named “geodatalytics_screenshot.png”. For both copied and saved screenshots, a camera flash animation will appear to indicate that the screenshot has been captured.
docs.title: Screenshot Menu

docs.text: The fifth icon in the controls bar is a button to automatically fit the bounds of the map to the set of currently visible layers. In this case, a “visible” layer is any layer that is added to the Selected Layers panel and does not have its visibility toggled off. A layer can be visible even if it is not in your current viewport. Keep in mind that if you have multiple visible layers, clicking this button will fly the map to a position that shows the union of the bounds of all of those layers. If your visible layers are geographically far apart, this button will likely be less useful. If you only have one visible layer, this button will autofit the map bounds to just that layer. This can be especially useful if you don’t know where the layer should appear on the map and want to find the location quickly. If you have not yet added any layers to the map, this button does nothing.
docs.title: Map Autofit

docs.text: The sixth icon in the controls bar is a button to toggle the application theme between light and dark modes.
docs.title: Theme Toggle

docs.text: The seventh and final icon in the controls bar shows a simple help menu when hovered. This help menu has a button to show a small tutorial of the interface, and it summarizes the map’s mouse and keyboard controls explained in the introduction above.

This can include climate simulations, computer vision, infrastructure analysis, and data generation. GeoDatalytics comes with a few pre-made tasks for basic use cases, but you may need to add other tasks for your use case. In order to add your own Analytics tasks, you will need your own application instance for which you have access to modify code on the server. Or, you can Contact Kitware for assistance integrating custom tasks. Architecture Analytics tasks are run asynchronously on a separate container, so long-running tasks will not interrupt the performance of the Django web server. When the web server receives a request to run an Analytics task, it will submit the task to a queue brokered by a RabbitMQ service. A GeoDatalytics instance can have one or more worker containers running a Celery service. The primary production instance of GeoDatalytics uses one celery worker hosted on an Amazon EC2 container. If you are managing your own application instance, you may wish to provision more than one worker according to your expected load. When a worker is not busy, it will pick up any tasks waiting on the RabbitMQ queue. It is essential to understand this architecture when implementing an Analytics task. The Celery worker that will run the task is separate from the web server and does not have the context of the request to run the task. However, both the Django web server and the Celery worker have access to the application’s PostgreSQL database. Thus, an Analytics task must rely on the database for loading inputs and saving outputs. Task Result Objects The TaskResult object is used to record the state of a running task in the database. The web client receives updates about the task whenever the TaskResult object is updated. During the execution of the task, the TaskResult object should be regularly updated with status messages and any error messages that may arise. The TaskResult object also stores the inputs and outputs of the task. When a user asks the server to start running a task, the server will synchronously process that request. It will first validate the task inputs; if an input is missing or incorrect, the request will receive a 400 Bad Request response with an informative error message. If all inputs are present and correct, the server will create a new TaskResult object, then spawn an asynchronous task with that object as an input, then without waiting for the asynchronous task, it will synchronously return the TaskResult object to the client. Since the client immediately receives the TaskResult object, it can immediately show the task status UI, even if the asynchronous task has not yet been picked up by a worker. The task status UI will show a loading bar with the initial status message until the task is picked up. When a worker starts running the task, it will start making updates to the TaskResult object that was passed as an argument. Those database updates will be propagated to the task status UI. When implementing a custom task, it is important to update the status as often as possible so the user receives more feedback. When the TaskResult object is marked as complete, the task status UI will show the object’s outputs. For Dataset and Chart outputs, a button will appear for the user to visualize the output (Datasets on the map and Charts in the Charts panel). Task Definition A task is defined in the server code with a Python class. Each task class is a subclass of the abstract class AnalysisType . The abstract class outlines the required attributes and functions that must be implemented in each subclass. Subclasses are defined in the same folder ( uvdat/core/tasks/analytics ). Each subclass should be registered in the __init.py__ file in that folder (without this registration, the task will not appear in the web client Analytics panel). Inputs and Outputs Subclasses of AnalysisType must specify inputs and outputs for the task. For outputs, an attribute output_types defines a mapping of all expected outputs and their types. Types can be basic data types (string or number) or certain GeoDatalytics objects (Dataset or Chart). A task can create other GeoDatalytics objects during execution, but they should be created with a relationship to a dataset. The task should return the dataset as output; this creates a uniform interface to visualize task outputs. For inputs, an attribute input_types defines a mapping of all expected inputs and their types. Types can be basic data types (string or number) or any GeoDatalytics object (Dataset, Chart, Layer, LayerFrame, FileItem, RasterData, VectorData). For GeoDatalytics object inputs, the user will select from a list of available objects of that type, returned by a query defined in get_input_options . The get_input_options function will return a mapping of valid choices for each input. This function is run when a user is requesting the form to spawn a new task of this type, so the options lists are dynamically generated. For inputs that should show a selection dropdown, return a list of objects that should appear in the dropdown (this could be a static list or a database query). For inputs that should show a numeric slider, return a list containing a single dictionary that defines the minimum, maximum, and step for the slider. For inputs that should show a freeform text input, return an empty list. Creating your own task As you implement your own task, it may be helpful to reference some examples. In the next section, a fake example is provided to highlight the most important points of these instructions. For specific use cases, you can find pre-made tasks defined in this folder . One of the examples in that folder, uncertainty_quantification.py , was contributed by one of our collaborators at the Sustainability and Data Sciences Laboratory at Northeastern University , written referencing this documentation. We recommend that you implement your custom task in the same folder, along with the pre-made tasks. Create a python file there with a unique, concise, and informative name. In that file you will define a subclass of AnalysisType and a Celery task function that will be called asynchronously. Note In order to register your task in your application, you will need to add it to the analysis_types definition in uvdat/core/tasks/analytics/__init__.py . Creating a subclass of AnalysisType You will need to provide the following attributes and functions: name : a unique, concise, and informative name (it is recommended to match the file name but with spaces and capitalization). description : This will appear as a tooltip next to the name in the list of analysis types. details (Optional): If specified, the UI for spawning this task will include an expandable “Details” section with this information. db_value : This is a unique string identifier for the task that will be stored in the database for every TaskResult object created for this task type. The database column is constrained to 25 characters, so this string must be under that limit (it is recommended to match or abbreviate the file name). input_types : A mapping of input variable names (camel case with underscores) to type strings. Valid type strings are “number”, “string”, “dataset”, “chart”, “network”, “rasterdata”, “vectordata”, “fileitem”, “layer”, “layerframe”, “region”, and "taskresult" (case insensitive). Input types other than “number” and “string” are database objects; the user will select from a list of available objects of that type, returned by a query you will define. input_defaults (Optional): A mapping of input variable names to default values. Not every input needs a default. If not specified, no inputs will have defined defaults, but the client application may select defaults for some inputs according to the user’s currently visible layers. optional_inputs (Optional): A list of input variable names. Input variables included in this list will be considered optional, so they will not be required in the task form. If not specified, no inputs will be optional; all inputs will be required. output_types : A mapping of output variable names (camel case with underscores) to type strings. Valid type strings are “number”, “string”, “dataset”, and “chart” (case insensitive). Your task can create other types of objects during execution, but they should be created with a relationship to a dataset. The task should return the dataset as output; this creates a uniform interface to visualize task outputs. attribution : A string listing the contributing institutions/individuals for this task. This is a way to provide credit to any third-party libraries or AI models you might leverage in this task. is_enabled : A function that returns a boolean value stating whether the task is available for users to run. This can just return true if the task is always available. Optionally, it could return a settings attribute if you would like to make a feature flag for enabling the task. If you do return a settings attribute for this, you will need to initialize that settings attribute in uvdat/settings/base.py . You can follow the same syntax used to define the other UVDAT_ENABLE_* settings attributes. You could also implement custom logic here if you have a more advanced use case. get_input_options : A function that returns a mapping of input variable names (camel case with underscores, matching the keys of input_types ) to lists of options. These could be static or dynamic lists, range specifications for numeric sliders, or a database querysets. Alternatively, an empty list will enable a freeform string input. The example implementation demonstrates each of these. Note that for database querysets, you may need to reference Django’s Queryset API documentation . validate_inputs (Optional): If this method is defined, you can perform additional validation on the inputs passed by the user. The superclass defines this method and will minimally check for the presence of all inputs. If you override this method, be sure to invoke the superclass implementation to first verify that all inputs have been provided. Then you can do some additional validations. If an input is invalid, raise an AnalysisInputError (a specialized exception type) with an informative error message. run_task : A function that creates a TaskResult object and spawns the asynchronous Celery task, passing the TaskResult object’s ID as an argument. You may pass additional arguments, but all arguments must be serializable (spawning a task will record a serialization of the function call to the task queue). This function should also return the TaskResult object so that the client can receive it. finalize : This method allows you to perform any last operations after the task has been completed (e.g. final status updates). Creating an asynchronous Celery task The function must have the shared_task decorator from Celery applied. This decorator will register the task and make it available to spawn asynchronously. You should also specify base=AnalysisTask as an argument to this decorator to ensure that your task will inherit base class functionality. Note: AnalysisTask is the superclass for the task function and AnalysisType is the base class for the task definition class. At minimum, the function should accept a result_id argument. At the start of execution, the task should get the TaskResult object from the database by its ID. The task should make regular status updates to that object. If an error occurs, an error message should be saved to that object. You may also choose to modify the object’s name and/or metadata during execution. Be sure to save the result object immediately after any updates so that the new object state will be reflected in the web client. The TaskResult object has some convenience functions for common updates: write_status , write_error , write_outputs and complete . These convenience functions already include a save statement. You can get the task’s inputs from the TaskResult object. Inputs that indicate a database object will only contain the ID of that object, so you must fetch the complete object from the database. If your task calls a function from an external library, be sure to install that dependency and lazily import it during task execution. To install the dependency and add it to the project requirements under the “tasks” extra, use uv add --optional tasks [dependency] (this should modify pyproject.toml and uv.lock ). You can import your dependency at the top of the task function, but not at the top of the whole file. Top-level imports of task dependencies will break tests and cause import errors on the web server. The test suite and web server do not have the tasks dependencies installed. If your task writes a file to disk, it is recommended to write that file to a temporary directory with the python tempfile library. In deployed application instances, you may not have control over the worker’s file system. To save the file’s contents to the database, you can create a FileItem object. The FileItem should be associated with a Dataset , which will be an output of the task. To make the dataset available for visualization, you must spawn a task to convert the dataset. The example implementation in the next section demonstrates this. If your task creates a chart as output, you will need to reference the ChartJS docs to populate certain fields. The chart_data value should adhere to the data structures schema and the chart_options should adhere to the options schema . Example Implementation The example code below demonstrates the most important things to note for implementing your own task. This code includes the definition of the AnalysisType subclass, as well as the definition of the asynchronous Celery task that is spawned by it (which uses the @shared_task(base=AnalysisTask) decorator). In this example, “My Custom Analytics Task” leverages a library called my_custom_task_dependency to segment anything from aerial imagery. The task takes five inputs: a text prompt, segmentation mode, threshold, number of epochs, and the imagery to segment. The task provides four outputs: the segmented polygons as a vector dataset, a chart showing the number of polygons segmented per epoch, an accuracy number, and a summary string. class MyCustomAnalyticsTask(AnalysisType): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.name = 'My Custom Analytics Task' self.description = 'A fake task for demonstrating implementation' self.details = 'An optional long string to provide more info' self.db_value = 'my_custom_analytics_task' # <25 characters self.input_types = { 'text_prompt': 'string', 'segmentation_mode': 'string', 'threshold': 'number', 'num_epochs': 'number', 'imagery': 'RasterData', 'region': 'Region', } self.input_defaults: { 'segmentation_mode': 'optimized', 'threshold': 0.5, 'num_epochs': 100, } self.optional_inputs = ['region'] self.output_types = { 'segmented_polygons': 'Dataset', 'epochs_chart': 'Chart', 'accuracy': 'number', 'summary': 'string', } # credit to institutions/individuals who contributed to this task # or third-party libraries/models self.attribution = 'Kitware Inc.' @classmethod def is_enabled(cls): # If this task is always available, simply return true # You may also choose to implement a feature flag for this task: return settings.ENABLE_MY_CUSTOM_TASK def get_input_options(self): return { 'text_prompt': [] # free string input 'segmentation_mode': [ # select from valid strings 'fast', 'accurate', 'optimized', ], 'threshold': [ # slider input {'min': 0, 'max': 1, 'step': 0.01} ], 'num_epochs': [ # select from valid numbers: 1, 10, or 100 10 ** exp for exp in range(0, 3) ], # perform a database query to get valid objects 'imagery': RasterData.objects.filter( dataset__category='imagery' ), 'region': Region.objects.all(), } # This override is optional; superclass defines a default implementation def validate_inputs(self, inputs): # Call superclass implementation first super().validate_inputs(inputs) # Then perform any custom validation. # The UI slider won't allow threshold values outside the specified # range, but a direct API call could provide an invalid value. # You could validate all inputs in a similar manner, # but this is just a minimal example. threshold = float(inputs.get("threshold")) if threshold < 0 or threshold > 1: err_msg = "Threshold must be between 0 and 1" raise AnalysisInputError(err_msg) def run_task(self, *, project, **inputs): text_prompt = inputs.get('text_prompt') # Create a TaskResult object to store task inputs, outputs, state result = TaskResult.objects.create( name=f'Segmentation of {text_prompt}', task_type=self.db_value, inputs=inputs, project=project, status='Initializing task...' ) # spawn an asynchronous task, pass in the TaskResult ID my_custom_task.delay(result.id) return result def finalize(self, result): # Format completion time in minutes instead of seconds seconds = (result.completed - result.created).total_seconds() minutes = seconds / 60 result.write_status(f'Completed in {minutes} minutes.') # After the class definition, define a task that can be run asynchronously # that accepts a TaskResult ID as the only argument @shared_task(base=AnalysisTask) def my_custom_task(result_id): import my_custom_task_dependency # lazy-import any dependencies # Get the TaskResult object from the database result = TaskResult.objects.get(id=result_id) # Get pre-validated inputs from TaskResult object text_prompt = result.inputs.get('text_prompt') segmentation_mode = result.inputs.get('segmentation_mode') threshold = result.inputs.get('threshold') num_epochs = result.inputs.get('num_epochs') # Inputs with object references will contain only the ID imagery_id = result.inputs.get('imagery') region_id = result.inputs.get('region') # Fetch the objects by their IDs imagery = RasterData.objects.get(id=imagery_id) region = None # Protect against None values for optional inputs if region_id is not None: region = Region.objects.get(id=region_id) # Make updates to the TaskResult object during execution result.write_status('Reading imagery...') # Get imagery data from RasterData object imagery_path = utilities.field_file_to_local_path( imagery.cloud_optimized_geotiff # field containing tiff ) result.write_status('Performing segmentation...') outputs = my_custom_task_dependency( imagery_path, text_prompt=text_prompt, segmentation_mode=segmentation_mode, threshold=threshold, num_epochs=num_epochs, region=region, ) segmented_polys_path, epochs_data, accuracy, summary = outputs result.write_status('Saving results...') # Create a new Dataset to represent the segmented polygons output dataset = Dataset.objects.create( name=f'Segmentation of {text_prompt} in {imagery.name}, description='Generated by My Custom Task', category='segmentation', metadata={ # Add any extra relevant info to metadata }, ) # Optional: add tags to the dataset dataset.set_tags(['segmentation', 'analytics']) # Optional: add the dataset to the result's project result.project.datasets.add(dataset) # Create a FileItem to store the file at segmented_polys_path file_name = 'segmentation.shp' file_item = FileItem.objects.create( name=file_name, dataset=dataset, file_type='shp', file_size=output_path.stat().st_size, ) # Save data from segmented_polys_path to FileItem with open(segmented_polys_path, 'rb') as f: file_item.file.save(file_name, File(f)) # Run dataset conversion; ensures data is visualization-compatible # For this example, the shapefile will be converted to GeoJSON. # Run synchronously so task is not completed before data is ready dataset.spawn_conversion_task(run_mode='sync') # Create a Chart object to store epochs_data chart = Chart.objects.create( name='Polygons Per Epoch', description='Generated by My Custom Task', project=result.project, metadata={ # Add any extra relevant info to metadata } ) # chart_data should adhere to ChartJS data schema chart.chart_data = { "labels": epochs_data['epoch_ids'], # along the x axis # one or more datasets of y data for each x label "datasets": [dict( data=epochs_data['num_polygons'], label='Number of polygons segmented', borderColor='#0000ff', backgroundColor='#0000ff', )] } # chart_options should adhere to ChartJS options schema chart.chart_options = dict( chart_title='Number of Segmented Polygons per Epoch', x_title='Epoch ID', y_title='Number of polygons', ) chart.save() # Record outputs on TaskResult result.write_outputs(dict( 'segmented_polygons': dataset.id, 'epochs_chart': chart.id, 'accuracy': accuracy, 'summary': summary, ))

For specific use cases, you can find pre-made tasks defined in this folder . One of the examples in that folder, uncertainty_quantification.py , was contributed by one of our collaborators at the Sustainability and Data Sciences Laboratory at Northeastern University , written referencing this documentation. We recommend that you implement your custom task in the same folder, along with the pre-made tasks. Create a python file there with a unique, concise, and informative name. In that file you will define a subclass of AnalysisType and a Celery task function that will be called asynchronously. Note In order to register your task in your application, you will need to add it to the analysis_types definition in uvdat/core/tasks/analytics/__init__.py .
docs.title: Creating your own task

docs.text: You will need to provide the following attributes and functions: name : a unique, concise, and informative name (it is recommended to match the file name but with spaces and capitalization). description : This will appear as a tooltip next to the name in the list of analysis types. details (Optional): If specified, the UI for spawning this task will include an expandable “Details” section with this information. db_value : This is a unique string identifier for the task that will be stored in the database for every TaskResult object created for this task type. The database column is constrained to 25 characters, so this string must be under that limit (it is recommended to match or abbreviate the file name). input_types : A mapping of input variable names (camel case with underscores) to type strings. Valid type strings are “number”, “string”, “dataset”, “chart”, “network”, “rasterdata”, “vectordata”, “fileitem”, “layer”, “layerframe”, “region”, and "taskresult" (case insensitive). Input types other than “number” and “string” are database objects; the user will select from a list of available objects of that type, returned by a query you will define. input_defaults (Optional): A mapping of input variable names to default values. Not every input needs a default. If not specified, no inputs will have defined defaults, but the client application may select defaults for some inputs according to the user’s currently visible layers. optional_inputs (Optional): A list of input variable names. Input variables included in this list will be considered optional, so they will not be required in the task form. If not specified, no inputs will be optional; all inputs will be required. output_types : A mapping of output variable names (camel case with underscores) to type strings. Valid type strings are “number”, “string”, “dataset”, and “chart” (case insensitive). Your task can create other types of objects during execution, but they should be created with a relationship to a dataset. The task should return the dataset as output; this creates a uniform interface to visualize task outputs. attribution : A string listing the contributing institutions/individuals for this task. This is a way to provide credit to any third-party libraries or AI models you might leverage in this task. is_enabled : A function that returns a boolean value stating whether the task is available for users to run. This can just return true if the task is always available. Optionally, it could return a settings attribute if you would like to make a feature flag for enabling the task. If you do return a settings attribute for this, you will need to initialize that settings attribute in uvdat/settings/base.py . You can follow the same syntax used to define the other UVDAT_ENABLE_* settings attributes. You could also implement custom logic here if you have a more advanced use case. get_input_options : A function that returns a mapping of input variable names (camel case with underscores, matching the keys of input_types ) to lists of options. These could be static or dynamic lists, range specifications for numeric sliders, or a database querysets. Alternatively, an empty list will enable a freeform string input. The example implementation demonstrates each of these. Note that for database querysets, you may need to reference Django’s Queryset API documentation . validate_inputs (Optional): If this method is defined, you can perform additional validation on the inputs passed by the user. The superclass defines this method and will minimally check for the presence of all inputs. If you override this method, be sure to invoke the superclass implementation to first verify that all inputs have been provided. Then you can do some additional validations. If an input is invalid, raise an AnalysisInputError (a specialized exception type) with an informative error message. run_task : A function that creates a TaskResult object and spawns the asynchronous Celery task, passing the TaskResult object’s ID as an argument. You may pass additional arguments, but all arguments must be serializable (spawning a task will record a serialization of the function call to the task queue). This function should also return the TaskResult object so that the client can receive it. finalize : This method allows you to perform any last operations after the task has been completed (e.g. final status updates).
docs.title: Creating a subclass of AnalysisType

docs.text: The function must have the shared_task decorator from Celery applied. This decorator will register the task and make it available to spawn asynchronously. You should also specify base=AnalysisTask as an argument to this decorator to ensure that your task will inherit base class functionality. Note: AnalysisTask is the superclass for the task function and AnalysisType is the base class for the task definition class. At minimum, the function should accept a result_id argument. At the start of execution, the task should get the TaskResult object from the database by its ID. The task should make regular status updates to that object. If an error occurs, an error message should be saved to that object. You may also choose to modify the object’s name and/or metadata during execution. Be sure to save the result object immediately after any updates so that the new object state will be reflected in the web client. The TaskResult object has some convenience functions for common updates: write_status , write_error , write_outputs and complete . These convenience functions already include a save statement. You can get the task’s inputs from the TaskResult object. Inputs that indicate a database object will only contain the ID of that object, so you must fetch the complete object from the database. If your task calls a function from an external library, be sure to install that dependency and lazily import it during task execution. To install the dependency and add it to the project requirements under the “tasks” extra, use uv add --optional tasks [dependency] (this should modify pyproject.toml and uv.lock ). You can import your dependency at the top of the task function, but not at the top of the whole file. Top-level imports of task dependencies will break tests and cause import errors on the web server. The test suite and web server do not have the tasks dependencies installed. If your task writes a file to disk, it is recommended to write that file to a temporary directory with the python tempfile library. In deployed application instances, you may not have control over the worker’s file system. To save the file’s contents to the database, you can create a FileItem object. The FileItem should be associated with a Dataset , which will be an output of the task. To make the dataset available for visualization, you must spawn a task to convert the dataset. The example implementation in the next section demonstrates this. If your task creates a chart as output, you will need to reference the ChartJS docs to populate certain fields. The chart_data value should adhere to the data structures schema and the chart_options should adhere to the options schema .
