docs.text: The example code below demonstrates the most important things to note for implementing your own task. This code includes the definition of the AnalysisType subclass, as well as the definition of the asynchronous Celery task that is spawned by it (which uses the @shared_task(base=AnalysisTask) decorator). In this example, “My Custom Analytics Task” leverages a library called my_custom_task_dependency to segment anything from aerial imagery. The task takes five inputs: a text prompt, segmentation mode, threshold, number of epochs, and the imagery to segment. The task provides four outputs: the segmented polygons as a vector dataset, a chart showing the number of polygons segmented per epoch, an accuracy number, and a summary string. class MyCustomAnalyticsTask(AnalysisType): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.name = 'My Custom Analytics Task' self.description = 'A fake task for demonstrating implementation' self.details = 'An optional long string to provide more info' self.db_value = 'my_custom_analytics_task' # <25 characters self.input_types = { 'text_prompt': 'string', 'segmentation_mode': 'string', 'threshold': 'number', 'num_epochs': 'number', 'imagery': 'RasterData', 'region': 'Region', } self.input_defaults: { 'segmentation_mode': 'optimized', 'threshold': 0.5, 'num_epochs': 100, } self.optional_inputs = ['region'] self.output_types = { 'segmented_polygons': 'Dataset', 'epochs_chart': 'Chart', 'accuracy': 'number', 'summary': 'string', } # credit to institutions/individuals who contributed to this task # or third-party libraries/models self.attribution = 'Kitware Inc.' @classmethod def is_enabled(cls): # If this task is always available, simply return true # You may also choose to implement a feature flag for this task: return settings.ENABLE_MY_CUSTOM_TASK def get_input_options(self): return { 'text_prompt': [] # free string input 'segmentation_mode': [ # select from valid strings 'fast', 'accurate', 'optimized', ], 'threshold': [ # slider input {'min': 0, 'max': 1, 'step': 0.01} ], 'num_epochs': [ # select from valid numbers: 1, 10, or 100 10 ** exp for exp in range(0, 3) ], # perform a database query to get valid objects 'imagery': RasterData.objects.filter( dataset__category='imagery' ), 'region': Region.objects.all(), } # This override is optional; superclass defines a default implementation def validate_inputs(self, inputs): # Call superclass implementation first super().validate_inputs(inputs) # Then perform any custom validation. # The UI slider won't allow threshold values outside the specified # range, but a direct API call could provide an invalid value. # You could validate all inputs in a similar manner, # but this is just a minimal example. threshold = float(inputs.get("threshold")) if threshold < 0 or threshold > 1: err_msg = "Threshold must be between 0 and 1" raise AnalysisInputError(err_msg) def run_task(self, *, project, **inputs): text_prompt = inputs.get('text_prompt') # Create a TaskResult object to store task inputs, outputs, state result = TaskResult.objects.create( name=f'Segmentation of {text_prompt}', task_type=self.db_value, inputs=inputs, project=project, status='Initializing task...' ) # spawn an asynchronous task, pass in the TaskResult ID my_custom_task.delay(result.id) return result def finalize(self, result): # Format completion time in minutes instead of seconds seconds = (result.completed - result.created).total_seconds() minutes = seconds / 60 result.write_status(f'Completed in {minutes} minutes.') # After the class definition, define a task that can be run asynchronously # that accepts a TaskResult ID as the only argument @shared_task(base=AnalysisTask) def my_custom_task(result_id): import my_custom_task_dependency # lazy-import any dependencies # Get the TaskResult object from the database result = TaskResult.objects.get(id=result_id) # Get pre-validated inputs from TaskResult object text_prompt = result.inputs.get('text_prompt') segmentation_mode = result.inputs.get('segmentation_mode') threshold = result.inputs.get('threshold') num_epochs = result.inputs.get('num_epochs') # Inputs with object references will contain only the ID imagery_id = result.inputs.get('imagery') region_id = result.inputs.get('region') # Fetch the objects by their IDs imagery = RasterData.objects.get(id=imagery_id) region = None # Protect against None values for optional inputs if region_id is not None: region = Region.objects.get(id=region_id) # Make updates to the TaskResult object during execution result.write_status('Reading imagery...') # Get imagery data from RasterData object imagery_path = utilities.field_file_to_local_path( imagery.cloud_optimized_geotiff # field containing tiff ) result.write_status('Performing segmentation...') outputs = my_custom_task_dependency( imagery_path, text_prompt=text_prompt, segmentation_mode=segmentation_mode, threshold=threshold, num_epochs=num_epochs, region=region, ) segmented_polys_path, epochs_data, accuracy, summary = outputs result.write_status('Saving results...') # Create a new Dataset to represent the segmented polygons output dataset = Dataset.objects.create( name=f'Segmentation of {text_prompt} in {imagery.name}, description='Generated by My Custom Task', category='segmentation', metadata={ # Add any extra relevant info to metadata }, ) # Optional: add tags to the dataset dataset.set_tags(['segmentation', 'analytics']) # Optional: add the dataset to the result's project result.project.datasets.add(dataset) # Create a FileItem to store the file at segmented_polys_path file_name = 'segmentation.shp' file_item = FileItem.objects.create( name=file_name, dataset=dataset, file_type='shp', file_size=output_path.stat().st_size, ) # Save data from segmented_polys_path to FileItem with open(segmented_polys_path, 'rb') as f: file_item.file.save(file_name, File(f)) # Run dataset conversion; ensures data is visualization-compatible # For this example, the shapefile will be converted to GeoJSON. # Run synchronously so task is not completed before data is ready dataset.spawn_conversion_task(run_mode='sync') # Create a Chart object to store epochs_data chart = Chart.objects.create( name='Polygons Per Epoch', description='Generated by My Custom Task', project=result.project, metadata={ # Add any extra relevant info to metadata } ) # chart_data should adhere to ChartJS data schema chart.chart_data = { "labels": epochs_data['epoch_ids'], # along the x axis # one or more datasets of y data for each x label "datasets": [dict( data=epochs_data['num_polygons'], label='Number of polygons segmented', borderColor='#0000ff', backgroundColor='#0000ff', )] } # chart_options should adhere to ChartJS options schema chart.chart_options = dict( chart_title='Number of Segmented Polygons per Epoch', x_title='Epoch ID', y_title='Number of polygons', ) chart.save() # Record outputs on TaskResult result.write_outputs(dict( 'segmented_polygons': dataset.id, 'epochs_chart': chart.id, 'accuracy': accuracy, 'summary': summary, ))

docs.text: Introduction Basic Controls Dataset List Structure Introduction The Datasets panel provides a list of all the datasets included in the current project, organized by category. Each category is an expandable section with a list of datasets. Each dataset is an expandable section with a list of layers. Clicking on any layer in the Datasets panel will add that layer to the map, as well as the Selected Layers panel for further configuration. This guide will explain the features available in the Datasets panel so you can explore the contents of your project. Basic Controls The main content of the Datasets panel is a hierarchical list of your current project’s contents. If you do not have a project selected, this panel’s list will be empty, and some controls will be invisible. The only visible controls will be the common controls present on every panel (see Panels ). This includes an expand/collapse icon, a drag handle for repositioning the panel, and a basic search box. Once you select a project at the top of the left sidebar (see Project Configuration ), the Datasets panel will update. Even if the selected project does not contain any datasets, the Datasets panel will show an additional control once a project has been selected. A blue plus button will appear in the header of the panel. Once clicked, that button will open the Project Management interface for the selected project, where you can add new datasets to the project (either by selecting existing datasets or creating new ones). You can also open the Project Management interface with the buttons next to the project selection box. Note If you are not logged in, you will not have access to the project management interface, so the blue plus button will not appear. Once the selected project contains at least one dataset, another control will become visible below the basic search box. You can expand the “Filter by tag” section to show a tag selection box. The tag selection box, when clicked, will open a menu listing the tags on all the datasets in the project. You can select multiple tags. Once a tag is selected, it will appear as a chip in the filter input. Each chip has an “X” button on the right, which, when clicked, will deselect that tag. When tags have been selected, the list of datasets shown in the Datasets panel will be filtered. Only datasets with matching tags will be shown. A dataset’s tags are shown as a list of chips under the dataset’s name when the dataset section has been expanded. The tag filters can be used in combination with the search filter to further narrow down the results. Dataset List Structure As stated in the introduction above, the dataset list has a hierarchical structure. At the top level are categories. These expandable sections contain datasets. In the screenshot below, the list shows the following top-level categories: transportation, elevation, imagery, region, amenities, and flood. Each category is displayed as a name and an up/down arrow indicating the expansion status of the category. The transportation, elevation, and imagery categories are expanded, each showing one or more datasets in that category. Each dataset is shown as a name, a set of icons, and an up/down arrow indicating the expansion status of the dataset. The following icons are shown next to each dataset name: A vertical three dots icon which, when clicked, opens a detail dialog. This dialog will display a table of basic information about the dataset, a list of related objects, and a table of metadata. a. Each item in the related objects list, when clicked, will show the details dialog for that related object. b. Downloadable items show a download icon; this icon will display a tooltip with the file size when the cursor hovers over it. Clicking the download icon will initiate a download of that file. A layers icon followed by a number indicating the number of layers the dataset has. An expansion arrow that points down if the dataset has not been expanded and points up if it has been expanded. When expanded, a dataset will also display the list of tags and the list of layers. Tags are shown as rounded chips, and Layers are shown as rows containing a blue plus button, the layer name, and a vertical three dots icon (which opens a similar details dialog when clicked). When the blue plus button is clicked, the layer will be added to the map and shown in the Selected Layers panel. You can add the same layer multiple times; numbered copies will appear in the Selected Layers panel, and you can apply different styles to each copy in that panel. See the Selected Layers Panel documentation for details.

docs.text: Introduction Basic Controls Comparison Mode Layer Style Menu Top Level Controls Color Tab Colormap Configuration Multiple Vector Feature Types Raster Options Size Tab Raster Options Filters Tab Raster Options Introduction As you add layers to the map from the Datasets panel , each layer will be added to a list in the Selected Layers panel. This panel is where you can manage layer visibility, ordering, styling, and advanced visualization modes. This guide will provide some basic examples of each, applied to some sample layers. Basic Controls The main content of the Selected Layers panel is a list of layers that have been selected from the Datasets panel. Each row in the list represents a single copy of a layer. You may add a layer to the map multiple times, and each copy gets its own row in the list. This allows you to compare different styles applied to the same layer. Note how in the screenshot above, the “libraries” layer has been added twice, and the second copy shows “(1)” next to the layer name. Each row in the list has the following five elements (left to right): A blue “X” button to remove the layer copy from the map and the Selected Layers panel. This will remove the row from the list. To get the layer back, you will need to add it from the Datasets panel again. A checkbox to toggle the visibility of the layer on the map. Unlike the blue “X” button, this will not affect the row in the list; it only affects the map. The name of the layer, along with the copy ID in parenthesis if this is not the first copy of the layer. The copy IDs are zero-indexed, so the first copy to show its ID has an ID of 1. A palette icon to configure the style for that layer copy. This will open the styling menu, which will be explained in the Layer Style Menu section. A reordering icon which communicates that the row can be dragged to reorder the layers on the map. You may grab the icon itself or anywhere else on the row that isn’t a control. Dragging a row to the top of the list will make it appear on the top of the layers on the map. Above the list of layers, there are a few additional controls that apply to all layers in the list for your convenience. The topmost blue “X” button will remove all rows from the list and remove all layers from the map. The topmost checkbox will toggle the visibility of all layers on the map. If any of the layers in the list have more than one frame, that row will have an additional frame slider control visible. This control consists of a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows. This enables you to scrub through the frames, increment one frame at a time, or enter a number to go directly to a target frame. The slider values are 1-indexed. Below the slider, the name of the frame is shown. In this case, the name of the first frame is “Frame: 0”, which is 0-indexed. Next to the name of the frame, a vertical three-dots icon is available to open a dialog with details about the current frame. You can toggle the visibility of these frame controls with the up/down arrow icon that appears next to the palette icon for multiframe layers. Like the other panels in the interface, the Selected Layers panel has a search box above the main content. Entering any text in the search box will filter the list of layers, showing only layer names that contain the search text. In the top-right corner of the panel, in addition to the basic panel control icons (see the Panel Controls section for more details on these common icons), the Selected Layers panel also has a split view icon which, when clicked, toggles map comparison mode. Comparison Mode When Comparison Mode is enabled, both the map and the Selected Layers panel are affected. The map will be split in two by a draggable divider. The two halves of the map are separate, but they move in sync as you pan and zoom. You can visualize different layers on each half of the map and swipe the divider to compare them. After clicking the split view icon, it will become blue to signify that Comparison Mode is enabled. It will also gain a subsequent icon below it which denotes the direction of the draggable divider. Hovering over the set of two icons will open a menu that allows you to set the direction of the divider (either horizontal or vertical). In the screenshot below, a layer depicting a simulated flood is shown on the top map, and a layer depicting the boundary of the river/bay water system is shown on the bottom map. The comparison divider can be moved down to show more of the simulated flood layer and moved up to show more of the water system layer. Underneath, an elevation layer is shown on both maps, unaffected by the comparison divider. Note that when Comparison Mode is enabled, each row in the Selected Layers panel now has two visibility checkboxes instead of one. Each checkbox controls the visibility of that layer on one side of the comparison map. When the divider is horizontal, the checkboxes control the top and bottom maps respectively. When the divider is vertical, the checkboxes control the left and right maps. Comparison mode can also be used to compare two different styles on the same layer copy. In the screenshot below, Only one layer copy exists in the Selected Layers panel, and it is marked as visible on both the left and right maps (both visibility checkboxes are checked). However, the left and right maps have different styles applied to the layer. Clicking on the palette icon next to the layer name opens the style configuration menu, which has a simplified interface when Comparison Mode is enabled. This simplified menu allows you to choose the style for each half of the map from a list of existing saved styles. The saved styles can only be created and configured with the full version of the styling menu when Comparison Mode is not enabled (see Layer Style Menu section). You can also adjust the opacity of the layer on each half of the map. The screenshot below shows this simplified style menu, where we can see that the left map has applied a different style called “highways”, where features are colored according to the “highway” property, which has values like “primary”, “secondary”, or “tertiary” for lines and “crossing”, “traffic_signals”, or “turning_circle” for points. The right map has applied the default style called “lanes”, where features are colored (with a different colormap) according to the “lanes” property , which denotes the number of lanes on a given road segment. The point features on this layer (representing intersections) do not have this property, so they are not visible with this style. One additional thing to note is that some tools in the Controls Bar are disabled when Comparison Mode is enabled. The screenshot tool and the ability to save a new bookmark are disallowed during comparison due to implementation constraints. Layer Style Menu The Layer Style menu can be opened by clicking on the palette icon next to any layer in the Selected Layers panel. This menu allows you to explore different styling options available for the target layer. You may save named styles for quick access, one of which can be set as the default style for that layer. The primary purpose of the style menu is to grant you the ability to create informative visualizations of your data. In the process of creating an informative visualization, you will need to explore what the data contains and experiment with your options. As you make changes to your style configuration, the layer will update on the map behind the style menu so you can immediately see the results of your changes. It’s important to note that the styling options available in the menu will differ depending on the content of the layer. The options available for vector data are different from the options available for raster data. While it is possible for a layer to have both vector and raster data, it is an uncommon and advanced use case. This guide will provide instructions for both vector and raster examples separately. The screenshot below shows the style menu for a raster-only layer, which depicts elevation values across the state of Massachusetts. This layer already has one saved style called “discrete terrain”, and this saved style is the default for this layer. The “discrete terrain” style has an opacity value of 0.3 and applies the “terrain” colormap in a discrete manner. The following sections will discuss each of these options and more. Top Level Controls The Layer Style menu is organized hierarchically. There are several top-level controls that will be discussed in this section. After the top-level controls, there are three tabs which control specific style attributes that are dependent on the data in the layer: the color, size, and filter tabs (discussed in the following sections) have different content for raster and vector data. But the top-level controls in this section are the same regardless of the data content of the layer. Note If you are not logged in, you will not have access to create or update styles, so some of the top-level controls will not be available. The first control is a selection box, which allows you to switch between saved styles. If no saved styles exist for a layer, the selection will appear like this: Once you have saved some styles for a layer, the selection options will be populated. There will always be one style marked as the default for a given layer. Selecting a saved style from this list will change the style of the layer on the map and will update the rest of the options in the style menu to reflect the configuration of that saved state so you can make changes if desired. Next to the style selection box is a pencil icon. Hovering over this pencil icon will display a menu with two options: rename and delete. When clicked, each option will open a corresponding dialog. Below the style selection box is a checkbox labeled “Set as default style”. This will automatically be checked for the first style you make. There can only ever be one default style for a given layer. Saving any style with this box checked will uncheck the box for all other styles on the layer. If the current layer has more than one frame, then an additional control for “Default Frame” will be visible. This value determines the frame that will be shown by default when the layer is first added to the map. This control consists of a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows. Next is the opacity control, which also consists of a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows. The maximum opacity is 1, and the minimum opacity is 0. This control allows increments of 0.1. After the color, size, and filters tabs (discussed in the following sections), the bottom of the Layer Style menu has three buttons: cancel, save, and save as new. a. The cancel button behaves the same as the “X” button in the top right corner of the menu; both buttons will close the dialog without saving changes to the current style. Even if you have unsaved changes, the state of the layer style will be maintained on the map and in the Layer Style menu the next time you open it. But those unsaved changes will not be maintained if you refresh the page. b. The save button will save the current configuration to the saved style you have selected at the top of the menu. If no saved styles exist, this button is disabled. You must use the "Save As New" button instead. c. The "Save As New" button will open a dialog prompting you to enter a name for the new style. After submitting the name, the new style will be created and will appear in the style selection box at the top of the menu. This is kept separate from the Save button so that you can make several variations of similar styles without re-entering common configuration values (e.g. you can select Style A, change one thing, and save it as Style B without changing Style A). Color Tab The color tab is the most complex tab with the greatest number of controls and the greatest degree of variation depending on the data content of the layer. This section will explain all of the possible controls that may appear in this tab, but you likely won’t see all of them for a single given layer. The options in the color tab are arranged hierarchically; only a few controls will be visible at first, but more may appear as you make decisions that prompt further configuration. For example, the screenshot below shows very little content in the color tab, prompting you for only a few decisions. These controls are shown for a vector-only layer that only has one type of feature (points only). The only controls visible are a checkbox to enable/disable prioritization of feature color properties (the tooltip next to the checkbox explains that “When enabled, features with fill and stroke properties will use those colors. Features without those properties will use the specified color configuration.”) and a color scheme selection. The color scheme selection has “single color” selected by default, so a color swatch next to the control shows the current single color being applied to all features (that do not have fill and stroke properties already). Clicking on the color swatch will open a color picker control so you can change the color. For this simple use case, these controls are all you need, so the color tab does not display any more controls. But if you switch the color scheme control to “colormap”, many more controls become visible. Colormap Configuration In the screenshot below, “colormap” has been selected, and the color swatch has disappeared, replaced by a set of more controls. Only the first control in that set is enabled; the others are disabled until the first control has a value. This is because you cannot apply a colormap to vector data until you specify which property to color by. The “Color by property” selection will have options populated according to the properties present on your data. In the screenshot below, these properties exist on points depicting the locations of hospitals in Massachusetts. Properties with string values, like “TOWN”, will display a label with few example values found for that property. Properties with numeric values, like “BEDCOUNT”, will display a label with the range of values that exist for that property. Once you have selected a property to color by, the other controls will become enabled. The next control in the list allows you to select a colormap. There are several built-in colormaps that will suffice to cover most use cases, but there is also an option to create a custom colormap for advanced use cases. Clicking on the “+ Create New Colormap” option will open a dialog where you can name and configure a new colormap. To configure a colormap, you will need to define a set of markers along a gradient. Each marker has a color and a value between 0 and 1. It’s important to note that every colormap is defined on a scale of 0 to 1, but it can be proportionally applied to any range. It can also be applied to a categorical property (like “TOWN” in the properties example above). The colormap configuration section is defined by a gradient bar with draggable markers along the bottom, followed by a list of the markers where each marker has a color swatch and a number control. The color swatches, when clicked, will open color picker menus that allow you to change the colors. To move the markers, you can either drag them along the bottom of the gradient bar, or you can modify the marker’s value with the number control. The values are synced, so changing one will change the other. To add a new marker, you can either click on any space along the gradient bar (hovering over the gradient bar will show where a marker will be created, as in the screenshot below), or you can use the “+Add” button at the bottom of the marker list. Once you create a custom colormap, it will be added to the colormap selection options and can be reused in other styles and on other layers in the current project (your colormap will not be available in other projects). After selecting a colormap, the following two controls determine how that colormap should be applied to the data. The colormap class control allows you to toggle between a continuous colormap versus a discrete colormap. The tooltip to the side explains that “A discrete colormap divides data into distinct, non-overlapping color buckets. A continuous colormap maps values along a smooth gradient.” When “continuous” is selected, the colormap is shown as a gradient. The control for the number of colors does not apply, so it is disabled. When “discrete” is selected, the colormap is shown with a finite number of distinct colors. The control for the number of colors applies for a discrete colormap, so it is enabled. Changing the value for this control will update the colormap with that number of colors. The last control in this set is for null values. This control determines how to render features that are missing a value for the selected property. By default, those features will be transparent (i.e. invisible on the map). Switching this control to “Single Color” will make a color swatch appear. Clicking on the color swatch will open a color picker menu so you can select a color for those features lacking a value for the selected property. That completes the explanation of the basic color controls, but as stated at the beginning, the options available will change depending on the data in the layer. The rest of this section will explain other variations of the color tab controls. Multiple Vector Feature Types If a vector layer has more than one type of feature (points, lines, or polygons), then an additional control will be shown at the top of the color tab. The checkbox labeled “Different color per feature type” is unchecked by default, so the default behavior is that the same color configuration will apply to all features in the layer. But if you check this box, you can specify a different color configuration for each type. Once the box is checked, an additional control will appear allowing you to select one feature type at a time. All of the usual color controls will now apply to only that selected feature type. You can switch between feature types as many times as you like and they will each maintain their own separate configuration. Next to the feature type selection box, an eye icon will also appear, allowing you to toggle the visibility of the selected feature type. Note that when you check or uncheck the “different color per feature type” box, the current configuration shown will be applied to all feature types. If the box is unchecked, only one color configuration exists; when you check the box, that configuration will be applied to all feature types until you make changes to differentiate the config for each type. If the box is checked, more than one configuration exists; when you uncheck the box, the current configuration shown (regardless of which feature type it is applied to) will become the configuration for all feature types. Raster Options When the target layer has raster data, the options vary slightly from the options available for vector data. When styling raster data, only the color tab is applicable; the size and filters tabs are not applicable to raster data. If the raster has multiple bands, the first control available will be similar to the “Different color per feature type” checkbox discussed above for vector data. The “Different color per band” checkbox, when checked, allows you to configure separate color styles for each band in the image. A band selection box will become visible, along with an eye icon to toggle the visibility of each band. When checked, the subsequent color controls will only apply to the selected band. Raster options have a similar “Color scheme” control, but it has one extra option. Rather than only choosing between a single color and a colormap, there is also a “None” option that is selected by default. The “None” color scheme will default to any inherent style present in the raster data. For example, an 3-band RGB raster will default to showing the first band in red, the second band in green, and the third band in blue. A single band raster will appear in grayscale. The single color mode operates the same way as it does for vector data. The colormap mode is mostly the same as for vector data, with a few key differences. Firstly, you do not need to select a property to color by; the colormap will be applied to the pixel values in the raster. Secondly, instead of a “Null values” control, there are two new controls: “Range” and “Clamping”. The range control, characterized by a slider with two handles and two numeric inputs with up and down arrows on either side of the slider, determines the minimum and maximum values to which the color map is applied. In the screenshot below, the target layer is a raster containing values in the range [-35, 270] , but the range slider indicates a range of [1, 100] . The selected colormap, “terrain” will be applied to this smaller range, meaning that the first color in the colormap, dark blue, will be assigned to 1, and the last color in the colormap, white, will be assigned to 100. The rest of the colormap in between will be assigned within that range. The clamping control determines how to render values outside the selected range. The tooltip next to “clamping” explains that “When enabled, values outside the selected range will be clamped to the ends of the colormap. When disabled, those values will appear transparent.” By default, clamping is enabled. In the example below, that would mean that values less than 1 would be colored dark blue and values greater than 100 would be colored white. But the screenshot below shows that clamping is disabled, so those values outside the selected range will be transparent. This concludes the explanation of the controls available in the color tab. Size Tab When discussing size as it applies to vector features, it is important to note that size refers to the radius of point features, the width of line features, and the width of the outline on polygon features. As with the color tab, the size tab will have a control that allows you to specify a different size configuration per feature type (if the target layer has more than one feature type). When the “Different size per feature type” checkbox is checked, a “feature type” selection box will appear, and the subsequent size controls will only apply to the selected feature type. Unlike the control in the color tab, though, this selection box does not have an eye icon to toggle the visibility of each feature type. Also similar to the color tab, the size tab is arranged hierarchically, so the visibility of certain controls will be determined by the choices you make for top-level controls, like “Size choice”. You can pick between a single size selection or a range of sizes. The single size mode is selected by default, so the following “size” control offers a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows to specify the size. This control accepts integer values 1-10. The last control visible for single size mode is the “zoom scaling” checkbox. The tooltip next to this control explains that “Size of features will change according to the current map zoom level, multiplied by a factor of the size value”. When zoom scaling is disabled, features will appear to have the same size on your screen regardless of the map’s zoom level. When it is enabled, features will appear to get bigger as you zoom in. If you switch to the “Range of Sizes” mode, more controls will become visible. The following control, “size by property” has a selection box of properties present on the data (just as with colormap mode in the color tab). The following controls, “size range” and “null values” are disabled until a property is selected. However, unlike the property selection in the color tab, this property selection control will only accept numeric properties as valid selections. In the screenshot below, the property selection options box shows only numeric properties. Once you have selected a property to size by, the size range and null values controls become enabled. Features with values in between will be sized proportionally in the specified range. The null values control determines how to render features that do not have a value for the selected property. By default, those features will be transparent (invisible on the map). You can also toggle this control to “size”, which will cause another control to appear with a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows. You can click the “+ Add New Filter” button to begin configuring your first filter. Clicking the button to add a new filter will create a group of controls in the filters list. Each filter in the list will consist of its own group of controls. The group of controls is fairly sparse to begin, but more controls in the group will become visible according to the choices you make. Each property will show a sample label with a few example values for string properties or a range for numeric properties. This allows you to test filter behavior by turning the filter on and off without removing the filter from the list entirely. Every filter you create will have this option; it essentially allows you to invert the behavior of the filter. The other controls in every filter will allow you to specify a set of conditions that a feature must meet to match the filter. By default, only matching features are shown on the map with the “include values” mode. But switching to “exclude values” mode means that matching features will be hidden and all other features will be shown. Once you select a property to filter by, more controls will become visible in the filter’s control group. Each option will have a checkbox next to it; you can check as many values as you like. If you select a numeric property (like “BEDCOUNT” in the screenshot below), then two controls will appear: “Value type” and “Values”. The value type control allows you to specify whether you would like to match a single value or a range of values. By default, range mode is selected, so the values control will show a range input, characterized by a slider with two handles and two numeric inputs with up and down arrows on either side of the slider. If single mode is selected for value type, then the values control will show a single value slider. Once you have finished configuring your first filter, you can add more to the list. To keep your filters organized, you can only focus one filter at a time. When a filter is focused, you can see the whole control group and can make adjustments. Other filters that are not focused will appear collapsed with a summary statement to describe the filter. Collapsed filters still show the eye icon and trash can icon for quick access, as well as one additional pencil icon. The pencil icon shown on a collapsed filter allows you to focus editing on that filter, which will expand the controls for that filter and collapse all other filters. If the current focused filter is empty (newly created with no configuration specified, as in the screenshot below), then that empty filter will be removed when you switch to focus on a different filter. Raster Options The filters tab is not applicable to raster data, so the tab will show a brief message instead of a control set when the layer only contains raster data.
docs.title: Selected Layers Panel

docs.text: As you add layers to the map from the Datasets panel , each layer will be added to a list in the Selected Layers panel. This panel is where you can manage layer visibility, ordering, styling, and advanced visualization modes. This guide will provide some basic examples of each, applied to some sample layers.
docs.title: Introduction

docs.text: The main content of the Selected Layers panel is a list of layers that have been selected from the Datasets panel. Each row in the list represents a single copy of a layer. You may add a layer to the map multiple times, and each copy gets its own row in the list. This allows you to compare different styles applied to the same layer. Note how in the screenshot above, the “libraries” layer has been added twice, and the second copy shows “(1)” next to the layer name. Each row in the list has the following five elements (left to right): A blue “X” button to remove the layer copy from the map and the Selected Layers panel. This will remove the row from the list. To get the layer back, you will need to add it from the Datasets panel again. A checkbox to toggle the visibility of the layer on the map. Unlike the blue “X” button, this will not affect the row in the list; it only affects the map. The name of the layer, along with the copy ID in parenthesis if this is not the first copy of the layer. The copy IDs are zero-indexed, so the first copy to show its ID has an ID of 1. A palette icon to configure the style for that layer copy. This will open the styling menu, which will be explained in the Layer Style Menu section. A reordering icon which communicates that the row can be dragged to reorder the layers on the map. You may grab the icon itself or anywhere else on the row that isn’t a control. Dragging a row to the top of the list will make it appear on the top of the layers on the map. Above the list of layers, there are a few additional controls that apply to all layers in the list for your convenience. The topmost blue “X” button will remove all rows from the list and remove all layers from the map. The topmost checkbox will toggle the visibility of all layers on the map. If any of the layers in the list have more than one frame, that row will have an additional frame slider control visible. This control consists of a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows. This enables you to scrub through the frames, increment one frame at a time, or enter a number to go directly to a target frame. The slider values are 1-indexed. Below the slider, the name of the frame is shown. In this case, the name of the first frame is “Frame: 0”, which is 0-indexed. Next to the name of the frame, a vertical three-dots icon is available to open a dialog with details about the current frame. You can toggle the visibility of these frame controls with the up/down arrow icon that appears next to the palette icon for multiframe layers. Like the other panels in the interface, the Selected Layers panel has a search box above the main content. Entering any text in the search box will filter the list of layers, showing only layer names that contain the search text. In the top-right corner of the panel, in addition to the basic panel control icons (see the Panel Controls section for more details on these common icons), the Selected Layers panel also has a split view icon which, when clicked, toggles map comparison mode.
docs.title: Basic Controls

docs.text: When Comparison Mode is enabled, both the map and the Selected Layers panel are affected. The map will be split in two by a draggable divider. The two halves of the map are separate, but they move in sync as you pan and zoom. You can visualize different layers on each half of the map and swipe the divider to compare them. After clicking the split view icon, it will become blue to signify that Comparison Mode is enabled. It will also gain a subsequent icon below it which denotes the direction of the draggable divider. Hovering over the set of two icons will open a menu that allows you to set the direction of the divider (either horizontal or vertical). In the screenshot below, a layer depicting a simulated flood is shown on the top map, and a layer depicting the boundary of the river/bay water system is shown on the bottom map. The comparison divider can be moved down to show more of the simulated flood layer and moved up to show more of the water system layer. Underneath, an elevation layer is shown on both maps, unaffected by the comparison divider. Note that when Comparison Mode is enabled, each row in the Selected Layers panel now has two visibility checkboxes instead of one. Each checkbox controls the visibility of that layer on one side of the comparison map. When the divider is horizontal, the checkboxes control the top and bottom maps respectively. When the divider is vertical, the checkboxes control the left and right maps. Comparison mode can also be used to compare two different styles on the same layer copy. In the screenshot below, Only one layer copy exists in the Selected Layers panel, and it is marked as visible on both the left and right maps (both visibility checkboxes are checked). However, the left and right maps have different styles applied to the layer. Clicking on the palette icon next to the layer name opens the style configuration menu, which has a simplified interface when Comparison Mode is enabled. This simplified menu allows you to choose the style for each half of the map from a list of existing saved styles. The saved styles can only be created and configured with the full version of the styling menu when Comparison Mode is not enabled (see Layer Style Menu section). You can also adjust the opacity of the layer on each half of the map. The screenshot below shows this simplified style menu, where we can see that the left map has applied a different style called “highways”, where features are colored according to the “highway” property, which has values like “primary”, “secondary”, or “tertiary” for lines and “crossing”, “traffic_signals”, or “turning_circle” for points. The right map has applied the default style called “lanes”, where features are colored (with a different colormap) according to the “lanes” property , which denotes the number of lanes on a given road segment. The point features on this layer (representing intersections) do not have this property, so they are not visible with this style. One additional thing to note is that some tools in the Controls Bar are disabled when Comparison Mode is enabled. The screenshot tool and the ability to save a new bookmark are disallowed during comparison due to implementation constraints.
docs.title: Comparison Mode

docs.text: The Layer Style menu can be opened by clicking on the palette icon next to any layer in the Selected Layers panel. This menu allows you to explore different styling options available for the target layer. You may save named styles for quick access, one of which can be set as the default style for that layer. The primary purpose of the style menu is to grant you the ability to create informative visualizations of your data. In the process of creating an informative visualization, you will need to explore what the data contains and experiment with your options. As you make changes to your style configuration, the layer will update on the map behind the style menu so you can immediately see the results of your changes. It’s important to note that the styling options available in the menu will differ depending on the content of the layer. The options available for vector data are different from the options available for raster data. While it is possible for a layer to have both vector and raster data, it is an uncommon and advanced use case. This guide will provide instructions for both vector and raster examples separately. The screenshot below shows the style menu for a raster-only layer, which depicts elevation values across the state of Massachusetts. This layer already has one saved style called “discrete terrain”, and this saved style is the default for this layer. The “discrete terrain” style has an opacity value of 0.3 and applies the “terrain” colormap in a discrete manner. The following sections will discuss each of these options and more.
docs.title: Layer Style Menu

docs.text: The Layer Style menu is organized hierarchically. There are several top-level controls that will be discussed in this section. After the top-level controls, there are three tabs which control specific style attributes that are dependent on the data in the layer: the color, size, and filter tabs (discussed in the following sections) have different content for raster and vector data. But the top-level controls in this section are the same regardless of the data content of the layer. Note If you are not logged in, you will not have access to create or update styles, so some of the top-level controls will not be available. The first control is a selection box, which allows you to switch between saved styles. If no saved styles exist for a layer, the selection will appear like this: Once you have saved some styles for a layer, the selection options will be populated. There will always be one style marked as the default for a given layer. Selecting a saved style from this list will change the style of the layer on the map and will update the rest of the options in the style menu to reflect the configuration of that saved state so you can make changes if desired. Next to the style selection box is a pencil icon. Hovering over this pencil icon will display a menu with two options: rename and delete. When clicked, each option will open a corresponding dialog. Below the style selection box is a checkbox labeled “Set as default style”. This will automatically be checked for the first style you make. There can only ever be one default style for a given layer. Saving any style with this box checked will uncheck the box for all other styles on the layer. If the current layer has more than one frame, then an additional control for “Default Frame” will be visible. This value determines the frame that will be shown by default when the layer is first added to the map. This control consists of a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows. Next is the opacity control, which also consists of a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows. The maximum opacity is 1, and the minimum opacity is 0. This control allows increments of 0.1. After the color, size, and filters tabs (discussed in the following sections), the bottom of the Layer Style menu has three buttons: cancel, save, and save as new. a. The cancel button behaves the same as the “X” button in the top right corner of the menu; both buttons will close the dialog without saving changes to the current style. Even if you have unsaved changes, the state of the layer style will be maintained on the map and in the Layer Style menu the next time you open it. But those unsaved changes will not be maintained if you refresh the page. b. The save button will save the current configuration to the saved style you have selected at the top of the menu. If no saved styles exist, this button is disabled. You must use the "Save As New" button instead. c. The "Save As New" button will open a dialog prompting you to enter a name for the new style. After submitting the name, the new style will be created and will appear in the style selection box at the top of the menu. This is kept separate from the Save button so that you can make several variations of similar styles without re-entering common configuration values (e.g. you can select Style A, change one thing, and save it as Style B without changing Style A).

docs.text: If a vector layer has more than one type of feature (points, lines, or polygons), then an additional control will be shown at the top of the color tab. The checkbox labeled “Different color per feature type” is unchecked by default, so the default behavior is that the same color configuration will apply to all features in the layer. But if you check this box, you can specify a different color configuration for each type. Once the box is checked, an additional control will appear allowing you to select one feature type at a time. All of the usual color controls will now apply to only that selected feature type. You can switch between feature types as many times as you like and they will each maintain their own separate configuration. Next to the feature type selection box, an eye icon will also appear, allowing you to toggle the visibility of the selected feature type. Note that when you check or uncheck the “different color per feature type” box, the current configuration shown will be applied to all feature types. If the box is unchecked, only one color configuration exists; when you check the box, that configuration will be applied to all feature types until you make changes to differentiate the config for each type. If the box is checked, more than one configuration exists; when you uncheck the box, the current configuration shown (regardless of which feature type it is applied to) will become the configuration for all feature types.

docs.text: When the target layer has raster data, the options vary slightly from the options available for vector data. When styling raster data, only the color tab is applicable; the size and filters tabs are not applicable to raster data. If the raster has multiple bands, the first control available will be similar to the “Different color per feature type” checkbox discussed above for vector data. The “Different color per band” checkbox, when checked, allows you to configure separate color styles for each band in the image. A band selection box will become visible, along with an eye icon to toggle the visibility of each band. When checked, the subsequent color controls will only apply to the selected band. Raster options have a similar “Color scheme” control, but it has one extra option. Rather than only choosing between a single color and a colormap, there is also a “None” option that is selected by default. The “None” color scheme will default to any inherent style present in the raster data. For example, an 3-band RGB raster will default to showing the first band in red, the second band in green, and the third band in blue. A single band raster will appear in grayscale. The single color mode operates the same way as it does for vector data. The colormap mode is mostly the same as for vector data, with a few key differences. Firstly, you do not need to select a property to color by; the colormap will be applied to the pixel values in the raster. Secondly, instead of a “Null values” control, there are two new controls: “Range” and “Clamping”. The range control, characterized by a slider with two handles and two numeric inputs with up and down arrows on either side of the slider, determines the minimum and maximum values to which the color map is applied. In the screenshot below, the target layer is a raster containing values in the range [-35, 270] , but the range slider indicates a range of [1, 100] . The selected colormap, “terrain” will be applied to this smaller range, meaning that the first color in the colormap, dark blue, will be assigned to 1, and the last color in the colormap, white, will be assigned to 100. The rest of the colormap in between will be assigned within that range. The clamping control determines how to render values outside the selected range. The tooltip next to “clamping” explains that “When enabled, values outside the selected range will be clamped to the ends of the colormap. When disabled, those values will appear transparent.” By default, clamping is enabled. In the example below, that would mean that values less than 1 would be colored dark blue and values greater than 100 would be colored white. But the screenshot below shows that clamping is disabled, so those values outside the selected range will be transparent. This concludes the explanation of the controls available in the color tab.
docs.title: Raster Options

docs.text: When discussing size as it applies to vector features, it is important to note that size refers to the radius of point features, the width of line features, and the width of the outline on polygon features. As with the color tab, the size tab will have a control that allows you to specify a different size configuration per feature type (if the target layer has more than one feature type). When the “Different size per feature type” checkbox is checked, a “feature type” selection box will appear, and the subsequent size controls will only apply to the selected feature type. Unlike the control in the color tab, though, this selection box does not have an eye icon to toggle the visibility of each feature type. Also similar to the color tab, the size tab is arranged hierarchically, so the visibility of certain controls will be determined by the choices you make for top-level controls, like “Size choice”. You can pick between a single size selection or a range of sizes. The single size mode is selected by default, so the following “size” control offers a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows to specify the size. This control accepts integer values 1-10. The last control visible for single size mode is the “zoom scaling” checkbox. The tooltip next to this control explains that “Size of features will change according to the current map zoom level, multiplied by a factor of the size value”. When zoom scaling is disabled, features will appear to have the same size on your screen regardless of the map’s zoom level. When it is enabled, features will appear to get bigger as you zoom in. If you switch to the “Range of Sizes” mode, more controls will become visible. The following control, “size by property” has a selection box of properties present on the data (just as with colormap mode in the color tab). The following controls, “size range” and “null values” are disabled until a property is selected. However, unlike the property selection in the color tab, this property selection control will only accept numeric properties as valid selections. In the screenshot below, the property selection options box shows only numeric properties. Once you have selected a property to size by, the size range and null values controls become enabled. The size range control, characterized by a slider with two handles and two numeric inputs with up and down arrows on either side of the slider, determines the minimum and maximum sizes to apply to the features. Features with values in between will be sized proportionally in the specified range. The null values control determines how to render features that do not have a value for the selected property. By default, those features will be transparent (invisible on the map). You can also toggle this control to “size”, which will cause another control to appear with a slider and numeric input with up and down arrows. Features that lack the selected property will be rendered with the size specified by this additional control. This concludes the explanation of the controls available in the size tab.
docs.title: Size Tab

docs.text: The size tab is not applicable to raster data, so the tab will show a brief message instead of a control set when the layer only contains raster data.

docs.text: The filters tab allows you to conditionally render vector features according to the values of certain properties. You can add as many filters as you like to a style, so the main content of the filters tab is a list. When you first visit the filters tab, that list is empty. You can click the “+ Add New Filter” button to begin configuring your first filter. Clicking the button to add a new filter will create a group of controls in the filters list. Each filter in the list will consist of its own group of controls. The group of controls is fairly sparse to begin, but more controls in the group will become visible according to the choices you make. So far, the group of controls for this filter includes a property selection box, an eye icon, a trach can icon, and a “filter mode” toggle control. These top-level controls will be available for every filter you create. The property selection box determines which property you want to filter by. If you would like to filter by multiple properties, you will need to create multiple filters. The options for this selection box are all the properties present on all vector features. Each property will show a sample label with a few example values for string properties or a range for numeric properties. String properties will have different filter controls than numeric properties. The eye icon toggles whether this filter is being applied. When clicked, the eye icon will show a slash through it and all the other controls in that group (besides the trash can icon) will become disabled. When the filter is disabled like this, it will not be applied to the data on the map. This allows you to test filter behavior by turning the filter on and off without removing the filter from the list entirely. The trash can icon will remove the filter from the list entirely, discarding all unsaved changes. The “filter mode” toggle has two modes: “include values” and “exclude values”. Every filter you create will have this option; it essentially allows you to invert the behavior of the filter. The other controls in every filter will allow you to specify a set of conditions that a feature must meet to match the filter. By default, only matching features are shown on the map with the “include values” mode. But switching to “exclude values” mode means that matching features will be hidden and all other features will be shown. Once you select a property to filter by, more controls will become visible in the filter’s control group. If you select a string property (like “TOWN” in the screenshot below), then a “Values” selection box will appear. The options in the values selection box will consist of all values found for that property across all features in the layer. Each option will have a checkbox next to it; you can check as many values as you like. If you select a numeric property (like “BEDCOUNT” in the screenshot below), then two controls will appear: “Value type” and “Values”. The value type control allows you to specify whether you would like to match a single value or a range of values. By default, range mode is selected, so the values control will show a range input, characterized by a slider with two handles and two numeric inputs with up and down arrows on either side of the slider. If single mode is selected for value type, then the values control will show a single value slider. Once you have finished configuring your first filter, you can add more to the list. To keep your filters organized, you can only focus one filter at a time. When a filter is focused, you can see the whole control group and can make adjustments. Other filters that are not focused will appear collapsed with a summary statement to describe the filter. Collapsed filters still show the eye icon and trash can icon for quick access, as well as one additional pencil icon. The pencil icon shown on a collapsed filter allows you to focus editing on that filter, which will expand the controls for that filter and collapse all other filters. If the current focused filter is empty (newly created with no configuration specified, as in the screenshot below), then that empty filter will be removed when you switch to focus on a different filter.

docs.text: Introduction Legend Structure Introduction The legend panel provides a visual overview of the current styles applied to your selected layers. This is a helpful panel to include in screenshots and bookmarks that you intend to send to others. The legend summary helps the viewer quickly understand what the layer styles convey about the data, without needing to inspect the style configuration menu for every layer. The legend is a read-only summary; see the Selected Layers panel to make changes to your selected layers and their applied styles. Legend Structure The legend mirrors the current state of the configuration you specify in the Selected Layers panel. The legend contains a list of layer style summaries, matching the order of the layers list in the selected layers panel. Each layer style summary is labelled with the layer name (and copy number if more than one instance exists). These labels match the labels in the selected layers panel, and they will appear in the same order. Each layer style summary illustrates the color configuration of the layer’s current style. Size and filter configurations are not included in the legend. Color configurations vary in complexity, so there are several variations of how a layer style summary is depicted. Single color applied to all features/bands Continuous colormap applied all features/bands. A label displays the name of the color-by property. If the color-by property is numeric, the colormap range will be displayed on either side of the color scale. Discrete colormap applied to all features/bands. A label displays the name of the color-by property. If applied to a categorical property, the color scale can be expanded to show the list of values that exist on the data and the color applied to each one. If applied to a numeric property, the colormap range will be displayed on either side of the color scale. (Vector only) Enable “Prioritize feature color properties” option. When this option is enabled in the color configuration, features with “fill” and “stroke” properties will be colored according to those property values. If some features lack those properties, they will be colored according to the rest of the color configuration, and the legend panel will display a label of “Use color properties; default to” above the color summary. If all the features in that layer have fill and/or stroke properties, the legend panel will only display the “Use color properties” label. Multiple color configurations (different configurations for each feature type on vector data and for each band on raster data). For each color configuration, the name will be displayed in bold, followed by the color summary, which can appear as any of the above variations.

docs.text: Introduction Example Networks Basic Controls Animation Configuration Menu Manual Animation Creation Conclusion Introduction GeoDatalytics is focused on modeling urban systems, so networks are essential to understanding the connectedness of infrastructure. Urban lifeline systems for water, electricity, transportation, etc. are spatially distributed across a set of connectors that can be represented as network edges and access points that can be represented as network nodes. Representing these systems with nodes and edges allows us to apply graph topology concepts for analysis and identify opportunities for improved connectivity that serves the community equitably. A network representation can be created for certain kinds of vector data; nodes are created for point features and edges are created for the line features that intersect those points. A separate edge is created for each segment of a line between two points. The Networks panel offers animation features that allow you to explore how the connectivity of a network is affected when some nodes go out of service. In the screenshot below, a network animation, generated by an analytics task, shows how the Boston subway system becomes disconnected when nodes are affected by an extreme flood event. Example Networks GeoDatalytics has a few built-in examples of transportation networks. The Boston subway system in the MBTA Rapid Transit dataset has a network representation (shown in the screenshot above), and this acts as a good example of a relatively sparse network for basic analysis. You can also create a more dense transportation network via the “Create Road Network” task, which takes a city name as input and will generate a network as output where intersections are nodes and the road segments between them are edges. These networks are much more complex, with a greater number of nodes and edges compared to the subway system. Road networks are also far more resilient because they have a greater degree of redundancy. The screenshot below shows only a portion of the road network created for Boston. These transportation examples demonstrate the basic network analysis capabilities, which can be applied to other interconnected urban systems. If your use case is focused on other types of urban systems and you would like help creating network representations of those systems, Contact Kitware so we can support your use case. Currently, creation of a network is only supported through the API or Analytics tasks . Basic Controls In the Network panel’s initial state, a list of available networks is displayed. A search bar allows you to filter the networks by name. Each network shows a vertical three-dots icon on the right. Clicking the dots icon will open the details dialog for that network, which will display some basic information and metadata. Clicking on the name of a network will add the network to the map (if not already shown) and show the main panel view. In the title section of the main panel view, the network’s name is displayed above a set of chips that provide an overview of the network. The first chip displays the network category, the second chip displays the number of nodes in the network, and the third chip displays the number of edges. Below the title section are the animation controls. If you have write access on the current project, then a button for creating an animation will be available. We’ll explore the controls for manual animation creation in the following subsection. For now, we’ll view an existing animation that was generated by the “Flood Network Failure” Analytics task (see Analytics Panel for more context.). The animation selection control offers a list of animations created for the current network. Once an animation is selected, additional controls appear and the network shown on the map will be recolored to visualize the first tick of the selected animation. In the screenshot below, the first tick of this animation only has 5 deactivated nodes (shown in red by the coast, where the flood intersects the network in the first hour of the flood event). Most other nodes in the network are all still connected, forming a single network component (shown in purple). There is one node that is not deactivated but it is surrounded by deactivated nodes so it is not connected to any other active nodes; this node is shown in black. When an animation has been selected, additional controls appear in the Networks panel. The first of these controls is a color bar that provides an overview of how nodes in the network are colored on the map. The sections of the color bar are sized proportionally to how many nodes are in that group. Hovering over a section of the colorbar will highlight that node group on the map and display a tooltip with the group name and node count. Below the color bar, an animation timeline slider is shown. You can jump to any animation tick using this slider. Or, you can use the set of play, pause, and rewind buttons that appear below the animation slider to automatically step through the animation at a regular interval. The network colors on the map and the color bar will update with each animation tick. As the network becomes more segmented by the deactivation of more nodes, each connected component will be assigned a color. The component groups are ordered by size in the color bar. Lastly, an expandable section of related objects is shown at the bottom of the animation controls (if the selected animation has any related objects). For animations generated by the “Flood Network Failure” task, the task result that generated it and the flood layer used are included as related objects. Each related object has a show/hide button next to it. If the related flood layer is shown on the map while viewing the network animation (like in the screenshots above), the flood frame will automatically be updated as the animation tick updates. Animation Configuration Menu The palette icon next to the animation selection control provides a menu with some options to configure how the animation is visualized. The time visualization mode control allows you to toggle how time is represented in your visualization. By default, time is visualized with the slider; you can move through time by manipulating the slider, and you can only ever see a single time step at once. If you switch to colormap time mode, then the slider will disappear. Some of the configuration options are not applicable in this mode, so those controls will disappear as well. In this mode, time is mapped to color, so all timesteps are represented with a static visualization. The node colors no longer represent connected components for a single time step; instead, a node is colored according to which timestep it goes out of service. If a node never goes out of service, then it will use the default node color. The colorbar still shows proportions of node colors, but now a color represents a state in the animation timeline. Color groups are not ordered by size, but by timestep index. Hovering over a color in the color bar will still highlight the nodes in that group and display a tooltip with the group name and number of nodes. The other controls in the animation configuration menu are as follows: Animation Interval (not applicable when mapping time to color). Interval in seconds between ticks when using the play or rewind buttons. Minimum 0.5 seconds and maximum 5 seconds. Colormap. Used to represent timesteps when mapping time to color, otherwise used to represent separate network components. Default node color. Used to represent nodes that never go out of service when mapping time to color, otherwise used to represent nodes that are not deactivated and not part of a component (single disconnected nodes). Highlighted node color. Used to highlight nodes in a group when hovering over a section of the color bar. Deactivated node color (not applicable when mapping time to color). Color used to represent deactivated nodes. Deactivated node opacity (not applicable when mapping time to color). Opacity of deactivated nodes. Manual Animation Creation While generated network animations are helpful for exploring simulated network conditions, it can also be helpful to manually specify network outages in a custom animation. Manual animation creation allows you to freely explore a network’s topology and present your discoveries to collaborators as an animated visualization. Note If you do not have write access on the current project, you will not be able to create network animations. The “+ Create Network Animation” button will not be visible to you. When the “+ Create Network Animation” button is clicked, an input will appear for you to enter the new animation’s name. The name must be unique among other animations for the same network in the same project. To submit, click the blue arrow button next to the input or press the “Enter” key. Once the animation has been created, it will be selected in the animation selection control. The animation will have a single state with no deactivated nodes, so the color bar will appear as all one color (since all nodes are included in a single connected component). The animation slider will only appear when the animation has at least two states. Buttons to “Delete State” and “Add State” will be available among the animation controls. Note Anyone with write access on the current project will be able to make changes to this animation. After clicking the “Add State” button, the slider will appear with two ticks. The new state will automatically be active. An instructive label at the bottom of the animation controls informs that you can “click any node on the map to find a button for toggling that node’s state”. Clicking on a node on the map will cause a tooltip to appear. As with any vector feature, the tooltip will display a table of properties. Below the properties table, a button to deactivate/reactivate the node is shown. Clicking the “Deactivate Node” button will cause the node and its connected edges to change color, using the deactivated node color selected in the animation configuration options. In the screenshot below, the deactivated node is shown in red. Additionally, after at least one node has changed state, the instructional label at the bottom of the animation controls will be replaced by a “Save & compute components” button. We’ll click this button after we deactivate a few more nodes. Once the “Save & compute components” button is clicked, the server will take a moment to compute the network’s connected components with the specified outage state. Once a response is received from the server, the visualization will update to color the remaining active nodes according to their component groups. The color bar will also be updated to reflect these node groups. The next time we add a state to the animation, the new state will be a copy of the current state. We can continue to add states, toggle nodes, and save changes to see the connected components. The “Delete State” button will show a confirmation dialog before deleting the current state from your animation. With these controls, you can manually create an animation with many timesteps to illustrate how the connectivity of a given network is affected by different outage states. Anyone else with read permission on the project will be able to view your animation and customize the visualization colors. Conclusion This concludes the explanation of the Network panel controls. While manually creating a network animation can provide some insight, a network animation can also be generated by an Analytics task. Tasks like these can be used to explore how a network would be affected by a particular scenario. Continue to the Analytics Panel section to see an example exploring how the connectivity of the Boston subway system would be affected during a simulated flood event.

An instructive label at the bottom of the animation controls informs that you can “click any node on the map to find a button for toggling that node’s state”. Clicking on a node on the map will cause a tooltip to appear. As with any vector feature, the tooltip will display a table of properties. Below the properties table, a button to deactivate/reactivate the node is shown. Clicking the “Deactivate Node” button will cause the node and its connected edges to change color, using the deactivated node color selected in the animation configuration options. In the screenshot below, the deactivated node is shown in red. Additionally, after at least one node has changed state, the instructional label at the bottom of the animation controls will be replaced by a “Save & compute components” button. We’ll click this button after we deactivate a few more nodes. Once the “Save & compute components” button is clicked, the server will take a moment to compute the network’s connected components with the specified outage state. Once a response is received from the server, the visualization will update to color the remaining active nodes according to their component groups. The color bar will also be updated to reflect these node groups. The next time we add a state to the animation, the new state will be a copy of the current state. We can continue to add states, toggle nodes, and save changes to see the connected components. The “Delete State” button will show a confirmation dialog before deleting the current state from your animation. With these controls, you can manually create an animation with many timesteps to illustrate how the connectivity of a given network is affected by different outage states. Anyone else with read permission on the project will be able to view your animation and customize the visualization colors.
