docs.text: Introduction Basic Controls Introduction The primary user interface of GeoDatalytics is organized into a set of six panels that are docked to the left and right sidebars by default. Other sections of this documentation will cover each panel in detail. This section will cover the basics of interacting with any of these panels. Basic Controls The title section of each panel includes the name of the panel, three icons, and a search bar to filter the content of the panel. The three icons shown in the upper right hand corner next to the panel title offer some basic controls for the visibility and positioning of the panel. The caret icon allows you to collapse the panel to a minimum height. Clicking the caret again will expand the panel to its default height. The dot grid icon is a handle to grab and drag the panel. Hovering over this icon will change the cursor to a repositioning icon. Click and hold the icon to undock the panel from its current sidebar and move it anywhere on the screen. Panels may be positioned over the map and act as floating panels; collapsing the sidebars will no longer affect their visibility when floating. When a panel is floating, an additional icon will appear in the bottom right corner. This triangular dot grid is another handle to grab the corner of the panel and drag to resize it. Hovering over this handle will change the cursor to a diagonal resize icon. Dragging a panel into either the left or right sidebar will snap the panel position to an available space in that sidebar, docking it. You can move the panel up and down within the sidebar to reorder the panels. Lastly, the “X” icon in the top right corner of a panel will close the panel, completely removing it from the interface. You can bring the panel back via the panel visibility menu available in the controls bar.

docs.text: Introduction Basic Project Controls Project Management Interface Structure Project List Dataset Selection Access Control Permissions Table Introduction Projects are the top-level structure for organizing data in GeoDatalytics. In order to start exploring data, you need to select a project. The project management interface allows you to create and configure projects. Project configuration involves dataset selection and access control. This guide will explain the features available in the project management interface so that you can get started with your own project in GeoDatalytics. Basic Project Controls When you first access GeoDatalytics, no project has been selected yet, so the map shows the whole world and the panels in the sidebars are empty. At the top of the left sidebar, just below the app title, there is a set of project controls. Note If you are not logged in, you will not have access to the project management interface, so some of the controls shown in these screenshots will not be available to you. The project selection dropdown controls the current project. If you already have access to one or more projects, the options in this dropdown will be populated with those project names. Selecting a project from the list will activate that project; the panels in the sidebars will be populated with objects in that project, and the map will zoom to the project’s default map position. If you do not have access to any projects yet, the project selection dropdown will display “No available projects.” You will need to create a new project in order to start exploring data on the map. To help new users, an informational tooltip is displayed when no projects are available in the project selection dropdown. To the right of the project selection, there are two icon buttons. The first button has a plus icon; when clicked, this button opens the project management interface and focuses the portion for creating a new project. The second button has a gear icon; when clicked, this button opens the same project management interface for general project configuration. If a current project is selected, an additional row will appear below the basic project controls. Two text buttons offer controls related to the project’s default map position. The first control, when clicked, will zoom and pan the map view to the default map position. The second control, when clicked, will set the project’s default map position to match the current map view. The latter control will only appear if you have write permission on the project. Project Management Interface Structure The project management interface has a list of all projects (that you have access to) along the left side. Once you select a project to configure from that list, then the main content of this interface is shown. The main content is organized into two tabs: Dataset Selection and Access Control. The following sections will explain each of these areas in detail. Project List The left side of the project configuration interface displays a list of all projects to which you have at least read access. If you have many projects, there is a search bar at the top of the list to filter the projects by name. Each project in the list can be clicked to select that project for configuration. In the screenshot below, the project called “My New Project” has been selected and is shown with a highlight. For each project in the list for which you are the owner, two icons are shown to the right of the project name. The pencil icon, when clicked, allows you to edit the name of the project. The trash icon, when clicked, will open a dialog asking you to confirm whether you want to delete the project. If you confirm, the project will be deleted. At the end of the list of available projects, there is a “+ New” button. When clicked, the button will be replaced with an input to specify a name for the new project. If you had opened the project management interface by clicking on the plus button instead of the gear button (see Basic Project Controls ), this input would already be visible and focused. Once you input a valid and unique project name, clicking the blue arrow button next to the input or pressing the “Enter” key will create the new project with you as the owner. That new project will automatically be selected for configuration, and the main content of the interface will show the Dataset Selection tab. Dataset Selection The Dataset Selection tab in the project management interface shows two columns: Project Datasets and All Datasets. This tab allows you to explore all the datasets available in the GeoDatalytics database and select relevant datasets for your project. After a new project has been created, it doesn’t have any datasets in it yet, so the left dataset list will be empty, as shown in the screenshot above. The screenshot below shows a project that has already been configured to include several datasets. Both columns show a list of datasets. Each dataset list has the same structure as the list in the Datasets panel. See the Datasets Panel documentation for a description of the basic dataset list controls. In addition to those basic controls, these dataset lists have a few more features. Any datasets that appear in the “Project Datasets” list on the left will show a blue “X” button to the left of the dataset name; clicking this button will remove the dataset from the project (and therefore remove it from that list). Any datasets that appear in the “All Datasets” list on the right will show at least one icon to the left of the dataset name, depending on the ownership of the dataset and whether it is included in the current project. Any datasets that you own will show a red trash icon which, when clicked, will show a dialog asking to confirm whether you want to delete the dataset. That dialog will also tell you which projects are currently using that dataset. If you confirm the deletion of that dataset, it will be removed from all of those projects and completely removed from the database. Every dataset that appears in the “All Datasets” list will show either a green checkmark icon if it has already been added to the current project or a blue plus button if not. Clicking on the blue plus button will add that dataset to the current project, and it will appear in the “Project Datasets” list. If you cannot find a dataset you need among the “All Datasets” list, there is also a blue “Upload New Dataset” button at the top of that list. If you do decide to upload your own dataset to GeoDatalytics, please use caution; all datasets are public and can be used by anyone. Visit the Dataset Upload documentation to learn more. Once you have added one or more datasets to your project, you are ready to start exploring and visualizing in the main interface. Or, if you would like to collaborate with other users on your project, you can complete the optional access control step. Access Control By default, a project can only be seen by its owner (and any site administrators). The access control tab in the project management interface allows you to grant permissions to other users. There are three tiers of access: owner, collaborator, and follower. For more details on which privileges are granted to each tier, see the Permissions Table at the end of this section. There can only be one owner of the project, typically the person who created it. The owner has read-write access and is the only one (besides site administrators) who can delete the project and assign access control. If you are the owner of a project, you will see a blue “Add Users” button at the bottom of the access control list. Clicking on this button will open a dialog to select users and specify the permission level for that set of users. You cannot add followers and collaborators at the same time; you must open the dialog again and specify a separate set of users at the other permission level. This constraint is in place to help users avoid accidental permission grants. If you add a user that already exists at another permission level, that user will simply be moved to the new permission level you specify. After submitting the permission assignments, the access control tab will show the users at each permission level. If you are the owner, you will also see trash icons to the right of each user which, when clicked, will show a dialog asking to confirm whether you want to remove that user from the project. If you confirm, that user will no longer have any access to the project, and it will not show up in the project list for them anymore. In rare cases, a project owner may wish to transfer ownership of the project to another user. The pencil icon to the right of the owner section allows the current owner to specify a new owner. Use caution when transferring ownership; you cannot undo this action. Only the new owner (or a site administrator) would be able to transfer ownership back to you. Once you transfer ownership, you will be demoted to collaborator on the project. docs.text: Introduction Dataset Creation Form Dataset Tags Dataset Metadata Layers Configuration Submitting The Form Dataset Processing Task File Conversion Layer Creation Introduction Datasets are the primary structure for organizing data in GeoDatalytics. Each dataset has one or more layers that can be visualized on the map. Each layer has one or more frames; most layers are single-frame, but multi-frame layers can be used to depict a third data dimension like time. Each frame can contain raster or vector data. GeoDatalytics is an open-science platform, so all datasets are publicly accessible. If you are uploading your own dataset, ensure that no private data is included. Projects are the organizational structure that allows you to group datasets together for a particular use case or study. See the Project Configuration documentation for more information about selecting datasets for a project. The project configuration interface is also where you will find the button to upload your own dataset. Note If you are not logged in, you will not have access to upload a new dataset. Dataset Creation Form Once you open the project configuration interface (see Project Configuration documentation), the Dataset Selection tab is open by default. At the top of the All Datasets list, there is a blue “Upload New Dataset” button. Clicking on this button will open a dialog with a form to enter information about the new dataset you will create. The first three fields in the dataset creation form are required. The dataset must have a unique name that is less than 255 characters. Ensure that the name you choose is descriptive and succinct. The dataset must also have a description; the description does not have a length limitation, but it should be about a sentence long. The description value will be shown in a tooltip next to the dataset name. The dataset must also have a category. The category input is a combobox, meaning that a dropdown will show available existing category values that you may choose from. But if you do not see any categories appropriate for your dataset, you may also create a new category. When you type a new category value into this input, a tooltip will appear to notify you that you will be creating a new category. As an example of how the name, description, and category values are used, the screenshot below shows a dataset as it appears in the dataset list. The dataset has the name “Boston Orthoimagery” and it belongs to the “imagery” category. Dataset lists are organized by category, so this dataset appears under the “imagery” collapsible section. The dataset row includes an information icon; hovering over this icon will show a tooltip with the dataset’s description. Dataset Tags The next input in the dataset creation form is the tag selection. This input is also a combobox, but unlike the category input, this input allows you to specify multiple values. When this input is focused, a dropdown appears with existing tag options. You may select any number of these existing values. You may also type a new tag into this input. The typed input acts primarily as a filter on the existing tags in the dropdown, but if no matches are found, you can press the enter key or unfocus the input to submit the typed input as a new tag. Once you do, a tooltip will appear to notify you that you will be creating a new tag. The tag will only be created in the database when you submit the form. As an example of how tags are used, the screenshot below shows the tag filter control on the dataset list. The filters control is collapsed by default but can be expanded to show a similar combobox control. You can type in the input to filter the dropdown and you can select one or more existing tags to filter the dataset list. This screenshot shows that the “boston” tag has been selected, so the dataset list is filtered to only include datasets with the tag “boston”. The dataset named “MBTA Rapid Transit” is expanded to show its tags and layers. Dataset tags are shown as chips. This dataset has three tags: “boston”, “network”, and “public transit”. Dataset Metadata You may optionally specify any other useful information about your dataset in its metadata. The metadata input is collapsed by default on the dataset creation form, but expanding it will show a JSON editor. Dataset metadata is a JSON value but is otherwise unstructured. You can add string, numeric, boolean, and nested values in this JSON. A dataset’s metadata is only shown in its details dialog, which can be opened by clicking on the vertical three-dots icon that appears to the right of the dataset’s name in the dataset list. In the details dialog, the metadata is shown as a structured table. Key names will have underscores replaced with spaces. Nested values will also be shown as a structured table. Layers Configuration At the bottom of the dataset creation form, there is a final section titled “Layers Configuration”. This is where you can specify the data contents of the dataset. As mentioned in the introduction above, each dataset has one or more layers. This section of the form allows you to create those layers, giving each one a name and file set. By default, this section shows a single layer to be configured, followed by a blue “+ Add Layer” button. Clicking this button will add more layers to the list. Only one layer in the list can be edited at a time, so other layers will be shown as collapsed sections. The collapsed sections show the layer name, a pencil icon, and a trash icon. The pencil icon will expand that layer for editing, collapsing all other layers. The trash icon will remove that layer from the list. For each layer in the list, you must specify a name (unique among the other layers on this dataset) and one or more files. The file input allows you to drag and drop or click to browse your local filesystem. The behavior of the file input will adapt to the number of files you select and the types of those files. Currently, the file input only accepts .json , .geojson , .tif , .tiff , and .zip files. The tooltip in the top right corner of the file input area says “Upload files to create a sequence of frames, or upload a single file to optionally split into frames.” As mentioned in the introduction above, each layer has one or more frames. When visualized on the map, multiframe layers will appear with a frame slider in the Selected Layers panel. If you upload multiple files to the same layer, each file will be treated as a separate frame. The frames will be ordered according to the file names, so it is recommended that you number them clearly. If you only upload a single file, an additional control will appear below the file upload. The tooltip to the right of this input says “Enter the name of an ordered feature property that corresponds to frame”. This means that you can split the vector features into frames according to a particular property. Each frame created will have a name that corresponds to a value for that property present in your data. For example, the features in your vector data file may have a “frame” property with integer values between 1 and 10. If you enter “frame” in the frame property input, your layer will have ten frames, each named with a number between 1 and 10. The frame slider for that layer will allow you to scrub through the frames in order. Each frame will show only the features that have the corresponding “frame” value. It is recommended that you should know the structure of your raster file before attempting to split it; some rasters are structured with multiple frames and/or multiple bands. One additional thing to note about the file uploads in the Layer Configuration section is that files are limited to a maximum size of 2 GB. Attempting to upload a larger file will result in an error, as shown in the screenshot below. This limitation exists to protect the application from abuse. If you have a need to upload larger datasets, please Contact Kitware so we can accomodate your use case. Submitting The Form At the bottom of the dataset creation form, there is a set of form controls. The first control is a checkbox labelled “Add dataset to current project”, and it is checked by default. If this control is checked when the form is submitted, then the created dataset will be automatically added to the project that was selected in the project configuration interface when you opened the form. If this checkbox is unchecked, you can always add the created dataset to your project later. Below the checkbox, there are two buttons. The “Cancel” button will close the form and discard your form inputs. The blue “Upload” button will submit the form and begin the dataset creation process. After submitting, the form will be closed and the dataset lists shown in the project configuration interface will refresh. Your new dataset will appear in the “All datasets” list (and in the “Project Datasets” list if the aforementioned checkbox was checked). The newly uploaded dataset will undergo a processing step, which may take some time depending on the size of the data. The following section explains more about this processing step. During the processing, the dataset will be shown with an animated loading circle beside the name (instead of any action buttons allowing you to add the dataset to the project or remove it). The dataset will be shown as having zero layers; the layers are being created as part of the processing step. Once the processing step is completed, the dataset list item will be updated to show the newly created layers on that dataset. The animated loading circle will be replaced with the appropriate icon or button according to the presence of the dataset on the current project. Since you were the one to create the uploaded dataset, you also have permission to delete it, and a red trash icon will appear next to the dataset name. Clicking on this icon will open a dialog asking you to confirm whether you want to delete the dataset. Dataset Processing Task When a new dataset is created, it must undergo a processing task which converts the raw data files to standardized formats and specialized database representations optimized for visualization and analysis. The dataset processing task consists of two steps: file conversion and layer creation. This processing task occurs in the background, so you can continue using the application while your dataset is processing. Once the processing task is complete, your dataset will be ready to visualize and explore on the map. All raster data is converted to Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF, or COG . This pyramidal TIFF structure stores different resolutions of the data to be shown at different zoom levels. This is why a raster layer will appear to have a lower resolution when the map is zoomed out, and it will appear to increase in resolution when you zoom in. All vector data is converted to GeoJSON , and a specialized database representation is created for each vector feature. These database representations store the geometry of the feature as a point, line, or polygon. Feature properties are stored as a JSON field. These feature representations are optimized for geospatial queries, such as the ones used to serve the tiles shown when you add the layer to the map. Other geospatial queries can be used within an Analytics task to get features by their location and properties. There are also special vector features that require an additional advanced representation. If a dataset depicts regions or networks, an additional processing step can be applied to represent the data with Region objects or a set of Network Node and Network Edge objects belonging to a Network object. These advanced representations are optimized for particular kinds of geospatial queries. The dataset upload form in the user interface does not cover this advanced use case, though, so Contact Kitware for support with these kinds of datasets. Layer Creation Once the data has been converted and specialized database representations of the data exist, the layer creation process will create a set of Layer and LayerFrame objects with references to the data representations. This process will create one or more layers on the dataset, and each layer will have one or more frames. These will be created in accordance with the configuration you specified in the dataset upload form. If you are creating a dataset via the API and fail to specify a layer configuration, a default layer configuration will be created automatically according to the dataset contents.

docs.text: Datasets are the primary structure for organizing data in GeoDatalytics. Each dataset has one or more layers that can be visualized on the map. Each layer has one or more frames; most layers are single-frame, but multi-frame layers can be used to depict a third data dimension like time. Each frame can contain raster or vector data. GeoDatalytics is an open-science platform, so all datasets are publicly accessible. If you are uploading your own dataset, ensure that no private data is included. Projects are the organizational structure that allows you to group datasets together for a particular use case or study. See the Project Configuration documentation for more information about selecting datasets for a project. The project configuration interface is also where you will find the button to upload your own dataset. Note If you are not logged in, you will not have access to upload a new dataset.

docs.text: Once you open the project configuration interface (see Project Configuration documentation), the Dataset Selection tab is open by default. docs.text: The next input in the dataset creation form is the tag selection. This input is also a combobox, but unlike the category input, this input allows you to specify multiple values. Once you do, a tooltip will appear to notify you that you will be creating a new tag. The tag will only be created in the database when you submit the form. As an example of how tags are used, the screenshot below shows the tag filter control on the dataset list. The filters control is collapsed by default but can be expanded to show a similar combobox control. You can type in the input to filter the dropdown and you can select one or more existing tags to filter the dataset list. This screenshot shows that the “boston” tag has been selected, so the dataset list is filtered to only include datasets with the tag “boston”. The dataset named “MBTA Rapid Transit” is expanded to show its tags and layers. Dataset tags are shown as chips. This dataset has three tags: “boston”, “network”, and “public transit”.

docs.text: You may optionally specify any other useful information about your dataset in its metadata. The metadata input is collapsed by default on the dataset creation form, but expanding it will show a JSON editor. Dataset metadata is a JSON value but is otherwise unstructured. You can add string, numeric, boolean, and nested values in this JSON. A dataset’s metadata is only shown in its details dialog, which can be opened by clicking on the vertical three-dots icon that appears to the right of the dataset’s name in the dataset list. In the details dialog, the metadata is shown as a structured table. Key names will have underscores replaced with spaces. Nested values will also be shown as a structured table.
